News.title: Prince Harry and Meghan Markle may only move back to the UK for six months before heading to Canada
News.content:
Prince Harry and Meghan Markle may only move back to the UK for six months before heading to Canada

Indeed, Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, are said not yet know exactly how long they intend to stay in the UK following their return next month

View 5 Images Prince Harry and Meghan Markle's return to UK may be shorter than expected (Image: PA)

Prince Harry and Meghan Markle could stay in the UK for as little as six months, it is claimed today. A source close to the Duke and Duchess of Sussex said their return may be just temporary, and they could be looking at a move to Canada or even Australia next.

‌



The source said: "It'll be an extended period of time. It could be six months, it could be a year, it could be more. I don't think even they know yet. They might suddenly go, 'Why don't we try Canada for a while?' “They love Canada. 'Why don't we try Australia?' It's one of the great things about having left the institution."

‌



Harry and Meghan are planning to relocate from the US later this month with their children; Prince Archie, seven, and Princess Lilibet, five, who are due to start at a co-educational private day school.

‌



Princess Catherine greeted with kiss at Royal Ascot, then people realise who it is READ MORE :

View 5 Images Prince Harry heading home with family - but might not be for ever says source (Image: AP Photo/Alex Brandon)

'The stars aligned'

Although the couple are understood to have privately discussed for a couple of years returning to the UK, they made their decision only a week ago when their children's places were confirmed at the school.

It is understood that the King was the first person they told.

‌



The insider told the Sunday Times: "The stars aligned: it's perfect timing in terms of the children's schooling, there appeared to be a good acting opportunity here [for Meghan] and also the draw of family not just being closer to the King, but the Spencers, with whom Harry is very close.

“He and his brother are not speaking, but there are other members of the royal family he remains close to."

View 5 Images Harry and Meghan are coming home (Image: IAN VOGLER/DAILY MIRROR)

‌



Prince Harry eyes Invictus Games

One royal source described the brothers' relationship as being "in cold storage and not coming out anytime soon."

The couple have made it clear they do not want the name of their children's school to be made public. And they want the location of their new home, which is a private, non-royal residence which will be outside London to be kept secret as well.

View 5 Images Prince Harry is pictured with his uncle Earl Spencer (Image: PA)

‌



The Mirror had reported last month how Harry, 41, was buoyed by an emotional reunion with the King when he visited the UK for Invictus Games events.

It is believed that the organisers of the sporting event - which was founded by the Duke of Sussex to help injured veterans - are planning to invite the monarch to take part in either the opening or closing ceremony, while also hoping he will attend a range of the sporting events to meet competitors.

View 5 Images Harry and Meghan wed in 2018 and, the following year, Meghan gave birth to Archie (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

And now it is believed Harry and Meghan will be in the UK for the games, which will take place near Birmingham next year. It is said the couple will reside in the Cotswolds, or close to Althorp, the Spencer family estate in Northamptonshire.

Princess Diana spent her teenage years there, and the Sussexes visited the estate with their children last month.

But it remains a mystery what Meghan, 45, will do for work here in the UK after a royal expert casted doubt over reported plans she will be in a Netflix drama called The Gentlemen.

News.title: Dog missing for nearly three weeks saved by mountain rescue team
News.content:
Dog missing for nearly three weeks saved by mountain rescue team

Teddy was missing on England's third-highest peak for three weeks before his barking was overheard by volunteers who brought him back safely to his relieved owner

View 3 Images Teddy was found by rescuers who heard barking (Image: Facebook/Keswick Mountain Rescue Team)

A dog has been rescued on a mountain nearly three weeks after he went missing during a walk.

‌



Teddy vanished on England's third-highest peak, Helvellyn, in the Lake District on August 2, sparking a frantic search. Volunteers heard barking on Friday and finally found Teddy stuck in Dry Gill, a steep ravine.

‌



Keswick Mountain Rescue Team (KMRT) and other volunteers helped Teddy off the mountain and were staggered to find, though he lost weight, had no significant injuries. A vet has assessed Teddy and now the pooch has been reunited with his relieved owner.

‌



KMRT, a rescue team based in the Cumbria market town, is funded through donations, and relies on the support of volunteers like those who found stranded Teddy.

5 dog breeds known for their intelligence and that are easy to train — full list READ MORE :

View 3 Images The rescue team found the pooch who had been missing for nearly three weeks (Image: Facebook/Keswick Mountain Rescue Team)

‌



KMRT said in a Facebook update on Saturday: "The team attended and reached Teddy, who thankfully had no obvious injuries, although after nearly three weeks on the fell, he had understandably lost a considerable amount of weight. He was given a small amount of food before being safely secured in a rucksack for the journey back down to Swirls car park.

"Around three and a half hours after the callout began, the team met Teddy’s owner and the original informant at Swirls, where Teddy was handed back to his very relieved owner for onward travel to the vets.

"A remarkable outcome after nearly three weeks on Helvellyn, and a huge well done to everyone who kept searching and never gave up on Teddy."

Article continues below

View 3 Images Teddy had lost weight while lost on the mountain (Image: Facebook/Keswick Mountain Rescue Team)

Photos shared by the KMRT showed a calm looking Teddy being placed into a backpack and carried down the mountainside and back to safety. Images showed the spectacular vistas before the team made it down the trail.

One snap also showed Teddy next to his missing poster that was placed on a bridge shortly after he went missing. KMRT said the rescue team of seven people took about 3 hours and 30 minutes.

News.title: Police ended chase seconds before car 'with cloned plates' crashed on A66 and killed 7
News.content:
Police ended chase seconds before car 'with cloned plates' crashed on A66 and killed 7

The IOPC said Cleveland Police officers ended their pursuit of a car just 10 seconds before it collided with a police car not involved in the chase, killing seven people

View 3 Images Doorbell footage appeared to show police pursuing a vehicle before the crash

The police watchdog has said Cleveland Police officers ended their pursuit of a car "believed to be using cloned plates" just 10 seconds before it collided with a police car not involved in the chase, killing seven people.

‌



The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said on Sunday afternoon that its investigators had verified some of the circumstances leading up to the crash, which happened on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, shortly after 3.30am on Saturday.

‌



Cleveland Police said a Volkswagen Passat was travelling the wrong way on the A66 when it collided with a police car.

‌



Two police constables - Matthew Blades, 37, and Tom Clough, 38 - were killed in the crash. The five occupants of the Passat - Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Cole Robert Worthy, 16, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Makai Saddington, 18 - also died.

View 3 Images From left to right: Makai Saddington, Theo Rae, Cole Robert Worthy, Michael Robert Cahill, Jakub Matusiak

The IOPC launched an independent investigation on Saturday morning following a mandatory referral from Cleveland Police.

‌



In an update on Sunday, the IOPC said an armed response vehicle began pursuing a Volkswagen Passat after officers received intelligence regarding "numerous incidents" linked to the vehicle.

It said: "Analysis of the police vehicle in car footage shows the pursuit lasted just under seven minutes before the Passat travelled onto the A66 in South Bank, against the flow of traffic, at which point the pursuit was aborted by officers and they continued to travel on the correct side of the carriageway.

"A short time after the pursuit ended, approximately 10 seconds later, the Passat collided with another police vehicle which was not involved in the pursuit but in the area to assist in a search for the Passat, believed to be using cloned plates that had activated an ANPR camera."

‌



View 3 Images The crash happened on the A66 in South Bank, near Middlesbrough, shortly after 3.30am on Saturday (Image: Teeside Live)

The police watchdog confirmed the names of the seven people killed in the crash.

Derrick Campbell, IOPC director of engagement, said: "Our thoughts continue to be with the family and friends and all those affected by yesterday’s collision. We recognise the devastating impact this incident has had on those in the force, the wider policing community, and the local community, and we offer our condolences.

Article continues below

"We have obtained initial accounts of officers involved in the pursuit, the incident log and in car footage of the incident. Work is ongoing to obtain additional material.

"IOPC investigators will continue to review and analyse all the evidence that is available to us. We will not be providing any further comment at this time."

News.title: Man rushed to hospital after 'collision with car and pedestrian' at Asda
News.content:
Man rushed to hospital after 'collision with car and pedestrian' at Asda

Emergency services were called to the Asda supermarket in Bangor, County Down following a report of a collision involving a car and a pedestrian

View 2 Images Emergency services were called to the scene (Image: NI Emergency Response Vids/Facebook)

A man has been taken to hospital after he was hit by a car outside an Asda supermarket.

‌



The incident took place at the Asda superstore in Bangor, County Down, in eastern Northern Ireland. Emergency services including Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI), Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service and Northern Ireland Ambulance Service were all called to the scene.

‌



The crash took place just before 1pm yesterday in the Market Square area of the seaside city, which is located 13 miles away from Belfast. The victim was a male pedestrian and he has been taken to hospital for treatment of his injuries, Belfast Live reports.

‌



View 2 Images The area was cordoned off for some time (Image: NI Emergency Response Vids/Facebook)

The area was cordoned off while enquiries were carried out but has since reopened.

Article continues below

A PSNI spokesperson said: "Police in Bangor are investigating the report of a collision involving a car and a pedestrian in the Market Square area of the city at approximately 12.50 pm today, Saturday 22 August.

"Officers and colleagues from the Northern Ireland Fire and Rescue Service attended the scene, and the male pedestrian was later transferred into the care of the Northern Ireland Ambulance Service for treatment of injuries. Part of the road was closed for a time as emergency services dealt with the scene, but has now reopened."

Anyone with information about or dashcam footage of the incident is asked to get in touch with the police, quoting incident number 608 of August 22.

News.title: Officer killed in wrong-way crash on A66 was excited to coach son's football team
News.content:
Officer killed in wrong-way crash on A66 was excited to coach son's football team

Husband and father-of-two Pc Matthew Blades, who was killed in the crash near Middlesbrough on the A66 yesterday, was preparing to start coaching his son's football team

A66 crash: Floral tributes laid as police cordon remains in place

One of two police officers killed in a crash that also took five other lives was a football coach looking forward to teaching his son, his club has said.

‌



Pc Matthew Blades, 37, and Pc Tom Clough, 38, were killed when a Volkswagen Passat that was travelling the wrong way down the A66 dual carriageway near Middlesbrough collided with their marked armed response vehicle that was going in the right direction.

‌



The five people who died in the Passat were Michael Robert Cahill, 23; Theo Rae, 17; Cole Robert Worthy, 16; Jacob Matusiak, 23; Makai Saddington, 18.

‌



Husband and father-of-two Pc Blades had recently become a Seaton Carew FC coach and was preparing for his first turn teaching its under-sevens Seahawks squad.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

Five teens who died in A66 police chase crash which killed two officers named READ MORE :

“He was looking forward to being part of the team and, most importantly, to coaching his own son, who is going to be playing for the Seahawks this season,” the club said on social media.

‌



“Matty and his oldest son are much-loved members of our club and our U10 Lions football family.”

Ex-frontline responder Graham Wettone, who served in the Metropolitan Police for more than three decades, said Cleveland Police staff “will literally know most people” in the force and the effect of the crash will be “massive”.

Cleveland police and crime commissioner Matt Storey also described the force as a “really tight-knit family” and said the incident “will have a big impact on them”.

‌



View 3 Images The scene after the fatal road traffic collision closed the A66 (Image: Iain Buist/Newcastle Chronicle)

Meanwhile Anna Turley, MP for the Redcar constituency where the accident happened, said the “whole community is reeling here today” on Sunday morning.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct investigating the lead-up to the crash at 3.39am on Saturday in South Bank, Middlesborough, after a mandatory referral from Cleveland Police.

‌



Officers had spotted a suspicious vehicle and a pursuit began before the car travelled onto the A66 and collided with a police car, the watchdog said.

It is understood the police vehicle Pc Blades and Pc Clough were travelling in was not part of the pursuit.

The families of the five males who were travelling in the Volkswagen are being supported by officers, Cleveland Police said on Saturday.

‌



View 3 Images Doorbell footage shows the police chasing a vehicle prior to the crash

In a statement to reporters on Saturday afternoon, Cleveland Police Chief Constable Victoria Fuller said: “These were brave officers protecting our communities and serving our residents who didn’t return home to their families at the end of their shift.”

The Cleveland police and crime commissioner, who represents areas including Hartlepool, Redcar, Liverpool and Stockton, told Sky News: “It’s my home, it’s where I’m from, and everybody knows everybody else... It is a small place, and the force is a really tight-knit family, really, and I think it will have a big impact on them.”

‌



MP Ms Turley paid condolences to the deceased and said the “whole community is reeling here today” on Sunday morning. Cleveland Police is a “close-knit” force and a “police family”, she added.

View 3 Images Floral tributes left by members of the public at the scene on the A66 in South Bank (Image: North News & Pictures Ltd)

“I know all of them are so professional they’ll be back on with their duties again today.”

‌



Cleveland Police Federation chairwoman Lauren Somerville said: “Words cannot describe the pain the Cleveland Police family are feeling today.

“Our colleagues who should have been going home to their loved ones at the end of their shifts are not. And that is just unfathomable.”

The tragedy prompted other police forces to send their condolences, including the Police Service of Northern Ireland, Sussex Police and the Met.

Article continues below

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said he was “devastated” to hear about the crash, while Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood said her thoughts were with all those affected.

News.title: Over 200 Brits have applied for asylum in Australia - but authorities tell them to stop
News.content:
Over 200 Brits have applied for asylum in Australia - but authorities tell them to stop

Brits trying back door route to stay in Australia by applying for asylum have been told they were getting 'seriously bad advice'

View 4 Images Sydney Harbour attracts the Brits (Image: Getty Images)

Over 230 British citizens have applied for asylum in … Australia! The latest figures from Down Under showed that cheeky Brits were using this route to try and extend their stay in the sunshine. Now the Aussie authorities have issued a formal warning that the UK applications must stop - because they would be rejected. So many have now been made they are included in official figures but still lag far behind countries like India and China.

‌



The government said that they had noticed UK and Irish temporary visa holders being advised on social media to apply for protection visas to extend their stay. The Department of Home Affairs called this is “seriously bad advice.”

‌



View 4 Images Australian authorities want to stem the tide of asylum applications from Britain (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke is finalising a plan for deterring “non-meritorious asylum claims”. Burke wanted to boost compliance by sending out more immigration officers to track down and deport overstayers exploiting the system.

The plans concerned some ministers who wanted to make sure it was not seen by migrant communities as an ICE-style, Donald Trump-like move, or weaponised by the Greens in a similar light.

View 4 Images Australian Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke (L) with Australian Governor-General Sam Mostyn (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Labour minister Chris Bowen said: “Australia needs an Australian immigration policy, not one from Donald Trump. Look at some of the countries on that list. Some of the countries on that list have provided Australia with wonderful migrants. Tony Burke is reviewing the entire migration programme, every stream of it, temporary and permanent, and he’ll have more to say.”

Burke’s prospective crackdown is being fiercely resisted by the Refugee Council of Australia, which has warned that stripping work rights and due process from genuine refugees would jeopardise the country’s humanitarian program.

‌



A spokesman said: “The answer to backlogs is better decision-making, not fewer rights. People seeking asylum must be able to work legally and support themselves while their claims are determined.

“Removing that right will instead increase the risk of poverty, homelessness and reliance on charities that are already under significant pressure.”

View 4 Images Uluru in Australia, which attracts tens of thousands of Brits each year (Image: Getty Images)

Article continues below

But the 198 applications that were reported from UK citizens in 2025-26 were a sign that the system remains susceptible to non-meritorious claims, given recent data suggests no UK citizens have been successful in their applications. An additional 32 people from the UK applied for asylum in July.

The increase in UK claims from September, October and November 2025, and March and April 2026, marked the first time that British applicants made enough applications to be publicly reported in department data.

There were also 105 protection visa refusals being contested by UK citizens in the Administrative Review Tribunal at the end of June, of which 87 had been launched in the last 12 months.

News.title: Stray cat has hilarious reaction after being called 'ugly'
News.content:
Stray cat has hilarious reaction after being called 'ugly'

The stray cat was only very young with a very distinctive yet unusual shade of 'diluted tortoishell' fur and markings - and she just 'showed up' at a cat lover's property

View Image The young cat has very distinctive fur and was called 'ugly' (stock image) (Image: Galyna0404/Getty Images)

A stray cat who “just showed up” at an animal-lover’s property had a strong reaction to being called “ugly”. Many people adopt cats all over the world, with felines being among the most popular choices of pet alongside the likes of dogs, aquarium fish, rabbits, and more.

‌



In fact, an estimated 10.8 million pet cats are owned by around 24 per cent of adults here in the UK. Cats are an appealing option for pets thanks to their ability to offer stress relief and provide companionship. They’re typically less consistently affectionate than dogs - though they can still be sweet and very tactile - and their sassy attitude is part of their charm for many.

‌



They’re relatively low-maintenance, and don't need walks like dogs do, which can make them more suited for those with busy lifestyles. Cats come in a variety of colours and hues, with a range of breeds becoming domesticated over the years. Occasionally, stray cats end up being adopted and go on to become essential members of the family.

‌



One woman took to TikTok to show off a very young stray cat with distinctive fur markings after she had wandered onto her property. Speaking directly to the camera while holding the cat, she said: “Look at this ugly little kitty, I love her. Um, she just, like, showed up.”

The woman then held the cat up to the camera, displaying the animal side-on - and the cat took the perfect opportunity to strike a pose. The cat extended out one front paw, raised her other front paw near her face and then turned her head and stared at the camera for a few seconds, just like a model on the catwalk.

This prompted the woman, who posts under the name ‘Kenxie’ to burst out laughing. In text written over the top of the clip, Kenxie penned: “She said ugly who.”

‌



How did people respond?

In the comments section, fellow TikTok users were keen to share their thoughts.

One person simply said: “Ugly? Excuse me?” and added a mock-up Vogue magazine with the cat on the cover.

Another posted a screengrab of Ben Stiller as the eponymous supermodel Derek Zoolander in the hit 2001 comedy film Zoolander. The character often performs a famous smouldering facial expression with a strong pout, referred to as “blue steel”. Alongside this image, the TikTok user quipped: “Wrong b**** try again.”

‌



A third asked: “Is she named Vogue?” While a fourth said: “What a diva.”

Content cannot be displayed without consent

The official BMW TikTok account said: “She ate and left no crumbs.”

Article continues below

And someone else added: “u have to name her madonna omg.”

But one person said: “Who calls a cat ugly? I mean, really like I’ve never heard someone who enjoys cats called them ugly.” Replying to this, Kenxie said: “Someone’s gotta keep her ego in check before she overthrows Love Island baddies.”

After the 10 second clip racked up more than 58.2 million views and more than 29,000 comments, Kenxie added: “Guys I only expected this to get maybe 10 likes how do I tell this icon she’s infamous without letting it get to her head.”

News.title: TUI flight issues urgent 'mayday' call above UK with fuel running low
News.content:
TUI flight issues urgent 'mayday' call above UK with fuel running low

The TUI flight from Cape Verde held over the Peak District for about 20 minutes but had to make an emergency landing at East Midlands Airport following an incident at Manchester

View 2 Images At least 17 flights were held over Manchester Airport with seven diverted (file) (Image: MEN MEDIA)

A TUI flight bound for Manchester was forced to make an emergency diversion as its fuel ran low.

The incident happened as flight BY439 from Aristides Pereira International Airport in Cape Verde was abruptly told to join a holding pattern over Manchester Airport before landing. This was due to a person "encroaching" onto the airfield at Manchester Airport on Friday night.

Greater Manchester Police confirmed a 17-year-old has been detained under the Mental Health Act and enquiries remain ongoing, Manchester Evening News reports.

The Boeing 737 MAX, which can accommodate up to 230 passengers, was told by Air Traffic Control to join the holding pattern while making its final approach as a result of the security breach.

View 2 Images The aircraft declared a general emergency by broadcasting squawk code 7700 (Image: @UseSquawk/X)

At least 17 flights were held above the airport while the incident was being resolved, while seven flights were diverted to other airports. Flight BY439 joined the holding pattern as instructed at 6,000ft over the Peak District but, after about 20 minutes of circling, its fuel started burning low.

Air Live reports the aircraft then declared a general emergency by broadcasting squawk code 7700. The 7700 squawk code is declared by pilots when an aircraft experiences an in-flight emergency that requires immediate priority handling and assistance from air traffic controllers.

Such emergencies include mechanical failures, onboard safety threats, medical emergencies or unclear or escalating situations. The code acts as a silent "mayday" which prompts air traffic control to clear airspace and alert emergency services on the ground. The aircraft is then guided to the nearest suitable runway.

The plane was diverted to East Midlands Airport, landing there shortly after midnight on Saturday, due to strict fuel limits and uncertainty about the length of the airfield closure at Manchester. The aircraft was then refueled and took off again about an hour after landing.

Manchester Airport re-opened to arrivals 15 minutes later. The flight from East Midlands Airport to Manchester Airport only took a brief 18 minutes and eventually landed at 1.35am on Saturday.

Angela Slater described her experience of being on board the TUI flight from Cape Verde. She wrote on Facebook: "Our flight from Cape Verde was one affected. Had to divert to the East Midlands, refuel and then come back to Manchester.

"Should have landed around 11.30pm instead [it was] 1.30am-ish, got home at 3.30am. But the flight [crew and captain] were amazing, kept us informed as much as they could and did what they had to do in a crazy situation.

Article continues below

"We didn’t have enough fuel to stay up in the air for an unguaranteed time. Think we did about 7 laps before diverting. Never ever seen so many planes up in the sky when actually been on a flight before."

The arrested individual was taken to hospital from the scene.

News.title: Police aborted pursuit about 10 seconds before fatal crash, watchdog says
News.content:
Police abandoned the pursuit of a car seconds before it crashed going the wrong way down a dual carriageway, killing all five men aboard and two officers, investigators have said.

Michael Robert Cahill, 23, Jacob Matusiak, 23, Theo Rae, 17, Makai Saddington, 18, and Cole Robert Worthy, 17, died when a Volkswagen Passat struck a Cleveland Police vehicle on Saturday on the A66 near Middlesbrough.

PC Matthew Blades, 37, and PC Tom Clough, 38, who were on the correct side of the road and were helping search for the car, were also killed.

The Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said the force had been pursuing the Passat following reports of "numerous incidents" linked to it.

The watchdog, which launched an immediate investigation, said the Passat was believed to be using cloned registration plates which activated an ANPR camera.

Analysis of footage from one of the police vehicles showed the pursuit lasted just under seven minutes before the Passat travelled on to the wrong side of the A66, at which point officers "abandoned" it, the IOPC said.

The pursuing officers continued to travel on the correct side of the carriageway but approximately 10 seconds later at about 03:39 BST, the Passat collided with the vehicle of PC Blades and PC Clough, who were "in the area to assist in a search" for the car, a spokesman said.

Security footage from a house on Lime Road in Middlesbrough appears to show a car being pursued by police vehicles three minutes before the crash.

News.title: CrossCountry cancels 'almost all' UK services after power cut
News.content:
Trains across the UK have been cancelled by rail operator CrossCountry after a power cut at its control centre.

The power outage started in Birmingham on Saturday and as a result, many of the systems used to manage the railway are unavailable, the operator said.

Cancellations are affecting most routes, from Glasgow to Penzance and Leeds to Manchester, until further notice because of "significant and unforeseen disruption", said CrossCountry, ranked Britain's worst rail operator, in June.

Transport Secretary Heidi Alexander said she was "concerned to hear about a power outage" and had asked publicly owned operators to provide "extra services where possible".

"We've also sent Network Rail power teams who are onsite and working to restore power and systems as soon as possible," she added.

Passengers are venting their anger on social media, saying the situation is the "worst case scenario" at the weekend, with some taking coaches before continuing their train journey with another operator.

Major routes between Manchester and Birmingham, which passes through Stoke-on-Trent, Coventry and Wolverhampton, along with routes from Leeds to York, Cheltenham to Cardiff and Glasgow to Edinburgh, are all affected.

CrossCountry confirmed tickets for Sunday would remain valid until Wednesday.

One user on X asked the operator if the situation would be resolved on Monday.

It responded: "We would hope so, but at the moment we have no further updates."

News.title: Robot boxing, football and sprinting at World Humanoid Games
News.content:
The second-edition of the World Humanoid Games is under way in China.

The competition, which kicked off on Saturday, will run for five days and has already included a robot running faster than Usain Bolt's 100m sprint world record.

Elsewhere at the event in Beijing, a robot performed Cristiano Ronaldo's iconic 'Siuuu' celebration on the football pitch and droids took part in synchronised marching at its opening ceremony.

Robots have also been competing in events including boxing, high jump, Tai Chi and table tennis.

The BBC's China correspondent Stephen McDonell reports from the country's capital.

News.title: ECB investigating England bowler Brydon Carse for 'nightclub incident'
News.content:
England bowler Brydon Carse is under investigation after he was reportedly involved in an incident at a nightclub in Derby on Saturday, the England and Wales Cricket Board has confirmed.

Videos circulating on social media on Sunday appeared to show Carse in handcuffs, being led away from a club by four police officers.

The Durham bowler, who is in England's squad for the second Test against Pakistan this week, was seen with team-mate Matthew Potts.

Carse, who is due to meet up with the squad on Monday, was not on England duty at the time of the reported incident.

"We are aware of an incident which is reported to have taken place in Derby last night, and are currently investigating," an ECB statement read.

"We will provide a further update when possible."

The ECB's investigation comes five days after England captain Joe Root urged his players to be "really good role models and human beings" at the start of his second reign as Test captain.

"You always want to represent your country in the best possible light," Root, 35, told BBC Sport.

"We might have fallen short of that on a few occasions in the recent past.

"The only thing we can do to rectify that is be really good role models, good human beings and put in really strong performances on the field."

England have endured a summer of turmoil, with former captain Ben Stokes announcing a shock retirement from international cricket and Brendon McCullum sacked as Test coach.

Off-field issues dominated last winter's tours, including an incident involving Harry Brook and a nightclub bouncer in Wellington and the team's drinking during a mid-Ashes trip to Noosa, culminating in a heavy 4-1 defeat by Australia.

The issues continued into the summer when Stokes broke a team curfew, setting in motion a chaotic six weeks that resulted in a 2-1 series defeat by New Zealand, Stokes' retirement and the sacking of McCullum.

Despite the issues, Root decided earlier this month to scrap the midnight curfew that was imposed in January.

Speaking to Sky Sports, Root said: "There's not going to be a curfew. I don't think this needs to be a big deal, to be honest."

Carse, who was born in South Africa, was suspended from cricket for three months in 2024 for historic betting offences.

He was banned after putting 303 bets on matches between 2017 and 2019, though he was not involved in any of them.

News.title: Mayors to get powers to overrule local councils on planning decisions
News.content:
Mayors across England will be given new powers to overrule local councils on some planning decisions.

The change would apply to proposals with more than 150 homes, more than 15,000 square metres of commercial space or buildings over 30 metres.

Mayors in 13 areas including Manchester, Liverpool, the West of England and the West Midlands will gain similar powers to Sir Sadiq Khan in London, who is already able to "call in" planning decisions.

Housing minister Matthew Pennycook said the powers were an "essential part of the toolkit that mayors need to effectively deliver new homes and regeneration".

The Conservatives questioned whether it was right for councils to lose the "ability to make planning decisions in their own communities".

The powers will also be available to mayors in the Combined Authorities in North East England, South Yorkshire, West Yorkshire, York and North Yorkshire, Hull and East Yorkshire, Greater Lincolnshire, Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, East Midlands, and Tees Valley.

Paul Bristow, the Conservative mayor of Cambridgeshire and Peterborough, told BBC Breakfast that if he had local powers, he would approve "tomorrow" a couple of blocked schemes that he said would "get new homes built that families could move into and charge economic growth".

Bristow said "it's not about overriding what local people want", but about developers and councils finding a compromise on projects instead of just saying no - which he believed the "perceived threat of intervention" would help.

In London, where Khan already has the power to review decisions on certain developments, external, housebuilding has fallen in recent years. But Pennycook insisted the "call in" powers had helped the mayor "unblock strategic growth sites" in the capital.

Bristow said if he had a similar local plan it would be "much more light touch" than London.

In the 2024 general election, the Labour government promised to build 1.5 million homes in England by the end of the decade, but housebuilders have warned the target could be missed.

Pennycook said the government was "absolutely determined to stick with that ambition".

He acknowledged the target was "really stretching" but said nearly 180,000 children were in temporary accommodation and "any smaller target wouldn't be commensurate with the scale of the challenge".

Bristow said the government has "no chance whatsoever" to meet its 1.5 million target.

"We need economic growth in this country, we need to get building and families need places to live, and at the moment, the planning system just isn't working."

In addition to gaining the new "call-in" powers, mayors are set to be able to grant "up-front permission", which the government says will allow building to begin "without a developer having to apply".

A consultation on how the powers will work is due to be published next week.

The government has sought to stress that local councils will continue to decide the majority of applications and that all decisions must still follow planning rules.

It has also said mayors will get a "bigger say" over how housing funding is spent in their area, with the government directing national agency Homes England to focus on local mayors' priorities.

New Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who served as mayor for Greater Manchester for nearly a decade, has repeatedly expressed his desire to transfer more powers to local mayors.

"Challenge does need to be made to local decision-making and actually it cuts both ways," he told the Sunday Times.

"Sometimes it's the other way round. It's the local authority putting forward something that's unacceptable in terms of the impact on the community. It's a two-way street."

Last month, Burnham promised to give all mayors a share of income tax revenue, saying he wanted to "bring power home" to "every postcode".

Earlier this week, he announced a secondment programme to send high-performing civil servants to work in mayoral offices.

The approach has faced criticism from some in his own party and the Liberal Democrats, who fear it could create a "two-tier system" that discriminates against those areas that do not have an elected mayor.

News.title: Scammers increasingly using QR codes to steal money and data
News.content:
When Les Howard could not find change for parking during a trip to the coast, a quick response (QR) code on the meter seemed to be the answer.

But the next day, the 61-year-old realised he had become the victim of an increasingly common scam as criminals started taking money from his bank account in Â£60 chunks.

Reports of QR code-related scams have gone up by 700% in the past four years, figures by Report Fraud have revealed.

Experts say criminals are finding different ways to exploit the codes as they become a common part of everyday life.

This could be disguising suspicious links in emails, gaining access to victims' messaging apps or convincing people who are out and about to download fraudulent apps to steal their money and data.

That is what happened to Howard, from Widnes, who was visiting Caernarfon in North Wales with his wife.

"We went to the car park where we normally go," Howard told the BBC Scam Secrets podcast.

"I normally have change in the car to pay for the parking, but this time I didn't.

"So there was a QR code to download and get an app and pay via an app."

News.title: How a new era of heatwaves could shake up the school calendar
News.content:
Over the past two weeks, the sound of children has returned to Scotland's school playgrounds. Their summer breaks began in late June or early July and ended in mid-August.

It's an academic year replicated in other European countries too.

In England, Wales and Northern Ireland, however, children will not return until early September. Their holidays are a similar length to Scotland's but England and Wales schools did not break up until late July, something that meant pupils were in school during the peak of the early summer heat.

Or at least they were meant to be in school. While it was 30C or more outside, inside many classrooms it felt far hotter. With no air conditioning and limited ventilation, the heat became stifling and more than 1,000 schools across the UK either closed or sent pupils home early before the hottest part of the afternoon. Conditions were particularly challenging for GCSE and Aâlevel students sitting exams during extreme heat.

Baroness Brown, chair of the UK's Climate Change Adaptation committee, has warned that "we know high temperatures can significantly impair concentration and performance" of children in schools.

Back in February 2026, Ofsted's chief inspector Sir Martyn Oliver said the timing of the school holidays should be reconsidered: "It's pretty hot usually in May, June and July, just at the point you're asking children to sit down and take an examâ¦ so I think there is a need to have a good old look at it [the school year]."

The recent hot weather has seen some parents join his call. Andrea Bigger, a parent in London, is "absolutely aware of the dangers" of extreme heat in classrooms. She says her daughter has previously suffered from heat exhaustion and was hospitalised after overheating at her primary school. She is "really concerned that the UK is not ready or prepared for this".

And this summer was not a one off. BBC analysis of temperature data shows a clear shift. In the 1960s, the first 30C day was occurring on average on 13 July. In the 2020s that figure has been 19 June.

News.title: Why we can't look away from hoarder home clean-ups
News.content:
Gordon says the main reason she posts online is to raise awareness, particularly about hoarding disorder and mental health.

According to the NHS, hoarding disorder is a mental health condition, external in which someone collects a lot of things and finds it difficult to get rid of them, even when they negatively affect their daily life.

"I think it's really easy to be quite judgmental," she says.

"People see footage of these homes online and in documentaries, and it's really easy to judge and think the person's lazy.

"There's a lot of stigma behind it and a lot of misunderstanding."

She says the stigma of being a hoarder can stop people from seeking help.

"This is real life. It's mental health. It's people who are finding themselves living in really unsafe, unsanitary conditions through no fault of their own.

"The more we can talk about it, the better. The less we judge, the more we can understand, [and that] is only going to be a good thing."

Gordon says many of her followers are hoarders themselves.

"I get a lot of messages in my inbox saying, 'Thank you so much for your content. That house that you did last week, mine's not dissimilar to that and you're making me feel like I'm not the only one that lives like this'.

"A lot of people have messaged me and said that, because they've seen my videos, they found the courage to ask for help or maybe hire a cleaner.

"So it is having a really positive effect."

Listen to highlights from Lincolnshire on BBC Sounds and Hull and East Yorkshire on BBC Sounds, and watch the latest episode of Look North.

News.title: Wicker Man director's sons complete their late father's film trilogy
News.content:
Robin Hardy always envisaged his iconic 1973 folk horror film The Wicker Man as the first part of a trilogy.

The Wicker Tree, released in 2011, brought him closer to that ambition, but his death in 2016 at the age of 86 left the project incomplete.

Now his sons, Justin and Dominic, have been able to complete their father's trilogy, after finding a script for the final film.

Wrath of the Gods has its premiere at the FrightFest horror festival in London, external on Friday, a family dream made possible thanks to the surprise discovery of some long-lost family archive.

"The person who bought Justin's old family home said they'd discovered six sacks of letters, scripts and other material pertaining to Robin Hardy and The Wicker Man in the attic," says Dominic, an art historian at the University of Quebec in Montreal.

"Justin's first instinct was to burn them, but we couldn't ignore this original source material. Although we left it unopened for six months or more."

News.title: Restriction zone scheme for offenders to start in October
News.content:
A scheme that could see serious sexual and violent offenders confined to areas just a few miles wide after leaving prison will be launched in October, Justice Secretary Alex Norris has announced.

Government ministers say this is designed to give victims greater freedom and further reduce the possibility of unwanted contact

The intention to introduce "restriction zones" for violent offenders who leave prison and who are on probation was first announced by the government last year.

Probation officers will be able to limit where serious offenders can go for as long as it is deemed necessary. Those who breach their new boundaries could be recalled to prison.

This would go beyond the current practice of imposing "exclusion zones" which ban offenders from specific locations such as a victim's home or place of work.

Norris is expected to come up with proposals to further restrict the early release of some prisoners when Parliament resumes next month.

But the Conservatives say that the best thing Labour could do to protect victims is to bring forward emergency legislation which would stop the early release of thousands of criminals.

There is a risk that serious sexual and violent offenders and victims could encounter one another outside exclusion zones.

The new scheme will specify confined areas for offenders in plans tailored to them and developed in consultation with victims.

Norris said the scheme would use GPS technology monitored by probation officers so that "those who step outside the boundaries can be quickly identified and face being sent back to prison".

"Offenders should carry the consequences of their crimes, not their victims," he added.

Amy Glover, director of domestic abuse services at Advance, a charity supporting women and girls who have experienced domestic abuse, praised the "change in focus".

However, she also called for reform to the criminal justice system saying many survivors of abuse chose "not to pursue a criminal conviction, and for those that do only 5% reach conviction."

A domestic abuse survivor named only as Kristina called the restriction zones a "fantastic concept" but noted that a perpetrator had continuously breached her indefinite restraining order "without consequence".

"The biggest challenge would be to gain victims' confidence in authorities to follow through their promises of protection," she added.

The announcement of the restriction zone scheme's start date comes after a change to the government's early release scheme following a backlash.

Introduced to ease prison overcrowding, on 4 August the policy was updated so people sentenced for rape, serious child sex offences and grooming would not be eligible for early release.

The Prison Governors' association warned this change to plans at a "very late stage" put further pressure on prison staff.

The restriction zone scheme was criticised when it was announced last year for potentially putting pressure on probation staff, something the government says it hopes to alleviate with more staff and a greater use of technology.

If you are suffering from domestic abuse, details of help and support in the UK are available at BBC Action Line

News.title: 'My skin makes me unique and I'm learning to embrace it'
News.content:
A woman born with a rare genetic skin condition that covers 98% of her body in birthmarks has spoken of how she is learning to embrace her appearance after years of trying to hide it.

Laura Kelly, 28, was born with congenital melanocytic naevus (CMN) and underwent 14 operations as a baby, with doctors fearing she may not live beyond the age of eight.

Laura said CMN made her self conscious about how strangers might react and that, growing up as a teenager, she often wore heavy makeup and planned outfits to cover her skin.

She said embracing how she looks and raising awareness of CMN has given her more confidence and hopes sharing her story will help others with a visible difference.

News.title: Climber Laura completes 'full house' of 1,072 peaks around UK
News.content:
It is a big day for Scottish climber Laura Baillie who has completed the "full house" of the UK's highest peaks.

Reaching the top of Carn na h-Easgainn in the Highlands, the 38-year-old becomes one of an elite group of about 100 people who have stood on all 1,072 summits.

To complete the Scottish Mountaineering Club challenge, hikers must tick off every Munro, Munro Top, Corbett, Graham and Donald in Scotland - as well as every Furth in England, Wales and Ireland too.

At 2,025ft (617m), Laura said she chose Carn na h-Easgainn as a simple final ascent so family and friends could be there to celebrate her achievement.

Even her 89-year-old granny was able to be there on the summit near Tomatin, south of Inverness.

News.title: Biker killed in Isle of Lewis crash
News.content:
A motorcyclist has died after a crash on the Stornoway to Ness road on the Isle of Lewis.

The crash involved a silver MG car and a black BMW S1000 RS motorcycle on the A857 near New Park, Newmarket, at about 16:40 on Saturday

Emergency services attended and the 56-year-old male rider was taken to Western Isles Hospital where he died. Nobody else was injured.

Police Scotland said the 44-year-old male driver of the car was arrested in connection with the incident and inquiries are ongoing.

News.title: Barbican Conservatory offers 2,000 free cuttings
News.content:
The Barbican Conservatory is offering free plant cuttings to the public, ahead of its three-year closure for restoration in January.

More than 2,000 plant cuttings will be available to people who have booked online on Wednesday, with two more opportunities to collect plants scheduled later in the year.

The Grade II listed arts venue is to undergo a Â£231m overhaul, including the development of a climate-controlled habitat to support plant health.

Barbican chief operating officer Dr Philippa Simpson said the conservatory restoration was focused on "creating a healthier home for plants and enabling more people to enjoy the environment and the activities it will host".

News.title: I'd swell up once a week - now my life has changed
News.content:
"It's changed my life. I can do everything I want to now. It's brilliant," says Jack Cope.

The 30-year-old joiner, from Bedford, has had hereditary angioedema (HAE), a condition which causes severe unpredictable swelling and painful attacks, since birth.

The swelling occurs all over his body, including in his throat, stomach and face. Even something as simple as using a hammer can cause his hand to swell.

But now, due to a trial at Addenbrooke's Hospital, in Cambridge, he is trying a new treatment which he says has massively reduced his symptoms.

"I was having about an attack a week and I've gone from that to nothing for nearly a year now," he says.

News.title: Iran-linked hackers behind cyber attack that shut down power plant, reports say
News.content:
A small power plant in the UK was shut down during a cyber attack.

The government said that at no point was there a risk to the UK's energy system, but the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) has contacted power companies to advise them about the risk of cyber attacks.

The Telegraph reported, external that the attack, which took place last month, was carried out by hackers affiliated to the Iranian regime.

For security reasons, neither the government nor the National Cyber Security Centre, which deals with attacks on critical infrastructure, would give further details of the site affected. However this was not an attack on an essential service such as a large power station.

According to the Telegraph, the power plant was shut down for four days.

DESNZ said the incident had affected a small-scale generator and at no point had there been a risk to the wider energy system.

The UK's power network has a number of smaller gas generators which provide short-term power when needed.

Protecting the country's supplies is a key challenge for the government. It is updating its regulations for cyber security, and working on a new energy resilience strategy for later this year.

Iran has long been regarded as a capable cyber power but while the Western cyber-security world is braced for attacks either from the state or hackers linked to the state as a result of its conflict with the US this year, there has been little activity so far.

News.title: Newcastle vs Liverpool LIVE: Elanga fires hosts in front after emotional Kevin Keegan tributes
News.content:
( Reuters )

Newcastle host Liverpool in the Premier League’s late kick off this afternoon with both clubs having undergone managerial changes in the summer break.

Eddie Howe departed as Newcastle boss following the sales of Sandro Tonali, Bruno Guimaraes and Anthony Gordon with his replacement Matthias Jaissle tasked with rebuilding the team this season. He faces a difficult opener with the Magpies winless in their last 19 top-flight encounters with Liverpool, though regime change at Anfield as well could present an opportunity to end that run.

Andoni Iraola takes charge of Liverpool having replaced Arne Slot. He will be hoping to bring the best out of Alexander Isak, who faces a hostile return to St James’ Park, and Florian Wirtz who underperformed in their first season with the Reds while also figuring out how exactly Liverpool can replace Mohamed Salah who has departed for Turkey. Iraola has himself admitted his squad was “thin” in some areas.

It is also set to be an emotional afternoon at St James’ Park as Newcastle and Liverpool join together to pay tribute to Kevin Keegan, who was a legendary figure at both clubs. Keegan passed away in July at the age of 75 and fans of both clubs will pay tribute before kick-off.

Follow all the action from St. James’ Park with our live blog below:

Manchester City produced a dramatic late fightback to snatch a 2-1 victory over Bournemouth in Enzo Maresca’s first Premier League match as their manager.

Josko Gvardiol grabbed a stoppage-time winner at the Etihad Stadium after Marc Guehi had cancelled out Marcus Tavernier’s first-half strike with an 84th-minute header.

It meant relief for Maresca in his first home match since succeeding Pep Guardiola at the helm.

open image in gallery Gvardiol’s late goal, given by VAR, come as a relief ( Getty )

Gvardiol’s last-gasp effort was initially ruled out for offside but the goal was given after a VAR check, prompting huge celebrations on the touchline.

Until then, Maresca had looked like being outdone by another new manager in Bournemouth’s Marco Rose.

Yet Maresca will feel victory was deserved after his side created a number of chances, with Erling Haaland – sporting a new close-cropped haircut – and Guehi spurning gilt-edged opportunities.

That Guehi put aside that miss to spark the turnaround was credit to him, having been deployed in an unfamiliar midfield role by Maresca.

That itself was an interesting statement by the Italian, whose arrival was greeted by a huge banner before the game.

This fed into a raucous atmosphere and City initially responded well, with Haaland playing Nico O’Reilly in on goal in the opening minutes and Phil Foden having a shot blocked.

open image in gallery Marc Guehi pulled one back for City ( PA )

open image in gallery Tavernier had fired Bournemouth in front ( Reuters )

A goal seemed inevitable but Haaland inexplicably missed from in front of goal after O’Reilly flew down down and picked him out with a pinpoint cross.

Yet as fans began to celebrate in anticipation, Haaland got his contact all wrong and the ball rebounded off him, allowing Bournemouth to escape.

They made the most of the reprieve and Rayan first served warning by pouncing on defensive uncertainty to force a save from Gianluigi Donnarumma.

City did not learn and failed to deal with a bouncing ball, allowing Rayan to turn and release Evanilson. He whipped in a cross to the far post and Tavernier made no mistake as he tapped in.

It took a last-ditch tackle from Gvardiol to prevent further damage but Haaland went close to levelling before half-time as Dorde Petrovic palmed away his glancing header.

Guehi, the unlikely partner for new signing Elliot Anderson in central midfield, spurned a better chance early in the second half when he turned a free header wide from a corner.

City stepped up the pressure with Antoine Semenyo testing Petrovic and Foden having a shot deflected before Haaland blasted over.

open image in gallery Erling Haaland had a frustrating afternoon (PA)

Haaland was denied again by Petrovic but Donnarumma had to be alert to keep out a Daniel Jebbison header.

City finally broke through when Guehi made firm contact with a header from a Rayan Cherki corner.

City sensed there was still time for a winner and Gvardiol delivered when he slotted home from a Cherki pass. A flag initially curtailed the celebrations but the goal was eventually given and the Maresca era is up and running.

Alexander Isak was unsurprisingly on the end of relentless boos from fans of former club Newcastle as he made his return to St James’ Park for Liverpool in their Premier League opener.

Isak forced a move out of Newcastle last summer, going on strike before eventually joining Liverpool for a record fee of £125m.

This burned bridges with the vast majority of the Magpies fanbase, who previously adored him for his goalscoring heroics over three seasons. The Swede also played a pivotal role in Newcastle’s first piece of domestic silverware in 70 years, scoring against Liverpool in a 2-0 Carabao Cup final win in March 2025.

Isak was unable to play in last year’s Tyneside meeting between the two teams due to injury, meaning Sunday’s season curtain-raiser acted as his first St James’ Park comeback as a Liverpool player.

The abuse was instantaneous for Isak as soon as he touched down at his former stomping grounds, with chants of “rat, rat, rat” being directed at him after he stepped off the Liverpool team bus.

After the announcement of Isak’s name was met with whistles, the 26-year-old kicked the game off to a chorus of boos from the centre-spot, which was a sign of things to come.

He continued to be jeered every time he received the ball and a crunching challenge on him, which left the striker hurt, provoked one of the largest cheers of the day from the home faithful, at that point second only to Anthony Elanga’s fifth-minute opener.

open image in gallery Isak was crunched by a Newcastle challenge which pleased the home crowd ( PA )

Magpies fans also aimed X-rated chants at Isak, singing: “There’s only one greedy b******”.

Isak, who scored 54 goals in 84 Premier League matches across his Newcastle career, will hope he can begin to replicate those numbers for Liverpool after injury and poor form led to a dud of a debut season at Anfield last term.

England cricketer Brydon Carse is under investigation following an incident at a nightclub where he appeared to be handcuffed by police.

The England and Wales Cricket Board (ECB) said the investigation is underway following an incident in Derby on Saturday night.

The Durham fast bowler is in England’s squad to face Pakistan in the second Test of their series at Lord’s this week.

Former England Test captain Ben Stokes, who is Carse’s team-mate at Durham, is also seen towards the back of the video.

His England and Durham team-mate Matthew Potts can also be seen talking to Carse while he is surrounded by four police officers.

"We are aware of an incident which is reported to have taken place in Derby last night, and are currently investigating," an ECB statement said on Sunday.

"We will provide a further update when possible."

It has been reported that Carse was not arrested and was released without charge. It is unknown what cause Carse to be detained by the police offers.

English cricket has been embroiled by several late-night incidents around bars and clubs over the last year.

Harry Brook was reportedly involved in a scuffle with a nightclub bouncer in Wellington the night before England played a ODI against New Zealand last October.

England’s Ashes Tour featured allegations of a “stag do” culture during their mid-series break in Noosa, where Ben Duckett was filmed seemingly intoxicated after hours.

Stokes and Gus Atkinson were then alleged to have broken curfew after the first Test against New Zealand this summer and were stood down from the second Test.

Joe Root, who has replaced Stokes as England captain following his retirement, subsequently abandoned England’s midnight curfew.

He told his England team-mates to “be adults, look after yourselves, look after each other”.

Carse has not played for England since the Ashes due to injury but could involved in the second Test against Pakistan this week.

The 31-year-old was an unused member of the squad as England wrapped up victory in the first Test against Pakistan in three days.

On Saturday, Carse was out celebrating Durham’s crushing Division Two victory over Derbyshire in the County Championship.

Carse took two wickets with Stokes starring with bat and ball in a 338-run win at Derbyshire with a day to spare. Potts finished with five for 46.

Durham have refused to comment on the incident, citing the ECB investigation.

News.title: Mariam Abu Dagga’s death in Gaza was a grievous injustice - those responsible must face the consequences
News.content:

Is it now a year since Mariam Abu Dagga, a Palestinian journalist who worked for Independent Arabia and the Associated Press, was killed by the Israel Defence Forces (IDF) in, of all places, a hospital. That fact is not in doubt.

The story, recounted in moving and forensic detail by the Independent’s Chief International Correspondent Bel Trew, is desperately sad and one of grievous injustice.

Mariam was 33 when she, journalistic colleagues and medical staff were hit by successive rounds of Israeli tank fire, leading to the suspicion that this was a “double tap” attack.

She leaves behind her teenage son, who she sent to the UAE for safety as the conflict intensified.

When Mariam was trying to get the truth about the war in a Gaza out to the wider world, she was also coping with the loss of her mother, who in the middle of the bombings in 2024 died of cancer, in part due to a lack of treatment.

Mariam had donated a kidney to her ailing father. Like almost every family in Gaza, they experienced bereavements and suffered multiple forced relocations. She always knew her own life was in especial danger, and understood the risks.

Her will had already been drawn up, and she was only too well aware of the way the IDF dealt with Palestinian hospitals, and that the one where she was based, the Nasser Medical Centre, would be soon surrounded by IDF armour.

So Mariam Abu Dagga was a selfless person and a devoted journalist who put herself in peril in a way few in the trade could ever hope, or wish, to emulate. She never gave up. Now, neither will friends and colleagues in pursuit of the truth.

Unsurprisingly, she and her family have been denied justice. Even by the standards of this merciless conflict, her death appears at the very least an act of extreme negligence by the IDF, and at worst it may have been something far more sinister.

In any case, the usual conventions of war were violated, as so often has been the case, according to the numerous indictments filed at the International Court.

The Independent has shared all our detailed findings with the Israeli military, and asked for comments on each point. The military declined to respond adding only that “the review is still ongoing under the General Staff Fact-Finding and Assessment Mechanism.”

An independent international inquiry is needed before it is too late to get at the truth.

Mariam was not, by any means, the only brave journalist to lose their life or suffer injury during the Gaza war. At least five journalists were killed in the assault on the Nasser hospital a year ago, and the Committee to Project Journalists (CPJ) says Israel has killed over 200 Palestinian journalists since 2023.

This is more fatalities than any other government has been responsible for since the CPJ began collecting data in 1992. It compares badly with the approximately 230 lost over the entire span of the US-led Iraq war between 2003 and 2011, and the 63 who died during the 20-year quagmire of Vietnam.

It is therefore worth considering whether the extraordinarily mortality rate for journalists in this war is linked to the fact that they are overwhelmingly Palestinians.

The Israeli government often complains that it is held to a higher standard than others. Yet it is precisely because Israel purports to be a free democracy with a responsible military operating within the Geneva conventions that it needs to account for itself, and is under increasing pressure to do so.

It is also, foolishly, resisting this, just as it is refusing to end its aggression in the West Bank and Lebanon, and to support President Trump’s efforts to extricate America from the war in Iran.

The Israelis seem to want to fight on and on and on, and don’t seem overly concerned about their methods or the counter-productive results.

The events since the October 7 massacres by Hamas, which was the worst atrocity of its kind since the Holocaust, have not left the Israeli people more secure.

The conduct of the war in Gaza, as well as the present campaign to drive Palestinians off their land in the West Bank and the destruction of southern Lebanon, is leaving Israel friendless in the world.

It has set back the Abraham Accords process which offered some hope of stability in the region. The future of Palestine remains unsettled, no matter what Benjamin Netanyahu might boast. He has even exasperated the Trump administration.

One step forward, and it is inevitable, is for Israel to allow international journalists access to Gaza. They cannot be excluded forever. What happens there is of global concern.

It is a war zone, but the media has almost always been present in when the bombs are dropping and bullets are flying, and it is a matter for them and individual journalists as to the jeopardy they think is a acceptable.

The more the world sees of the way Israel tries and fails to use military means to resolve a political dispute the more it will leave Israel isolated - and vulnerable. That, presumably, is why the Israeli government resists transparency - and it is not out of some altruistic concern for reporters.

Exposing the truth and telling the story in an unbiased, independent way is one of the reasons why the media is so essential even - especially - on the field of conflict; and no journalist identified as such should be killed just for doing their job.

What happened to Mariam and the others was wrong, and those who did it need to face the consequences.

Musicians at the Boston Symphony Orchestra voted Saturday to authorize the ensemble's first strike in 145 years.

The Boston Musicians' Association announced the vote before the union's three-year contract expires at 11: 59 p.m. Sunday.

Tensions rose in March when BSO decided to force out music director Andris Nelsons next summer after 13 seasons.

"In spite of the turmoil of the last six months caused by BSO’s leadership decision to terminate the orchestra’s musical director, Andris Nelsons, they have failed to agree to a collective bargaining agreement that would begin to restore the trust that they have destroyed and offer a fair contract to the musicians who are at the heart and soul of the BSO," the union said in a statement.

Management has not accepted a proposal for a mediator, the union said.

"We respect the musicians’ right to take this step as part of the negotiating process," BSO CEO Chad Smith said in a statement.

"Our focus remains on the negotiations and the ongoing constructive conversations. We are committed to reaching an agreement with competitive pay and benefits that enhances collaboration with the players," Smith said.

open image in gallery ( AP )

The orchestra's season opens Sept. 17.

Nelson, a Grammy Award-winning artist, began his tenure in Boston at the start of the 2014-2015 season and was appointed Gewandhauskapellmeister in Leipzig in February 2018.

open image in gallery Boston Symphony Orchestra building ( Getty Images )

The Boston Symphony Orchestra gave its inaugural concert on October 22, 1881, under Georg Henschel, who remained conductor until 1884. Henschel, a Civil War veteran, envisioned a great and permanent orchestra in his hometown of Boston.

For nearly twenty years, BSO concerts were held in the old Boston Music Hall; Symphony Hall, now one of the world’s most revered concert halls, opened on October 15, 1900
