World.title: Atiku’s subsidy u-turn: The bankruptcy of desperate ambition, By Sunday Dare
World.content:
To entertain Atiku’s hollow promise is to invite national economic suicide. The old import subsidy regime was not merely a pricing mechanism; it was a black hole of rent-seeking, round-tripping, and monumental corruption that starved health, education, and infrastructure of vital capital… Restoring it would instantly sabotage the nascent renaissance of local refining, crush private sector confidence, and plunge the country back into chronic foreign exchange haemorrhage.

In the architecture of modern political opportunism, few spectacles rival the breathtaking hypocrisy of Alhaji Atiku Abubakar’s recent policy pivot.

To watch a self-styled statesman — who less than four years ago cast himself as an uncompromising apostle of market-driven reform — scramble to promise the reintroduction of petrol subsidies is nothing short of political apostasy.

This isn’t merely a tactical policy disagreement; it is a sordid, stingy manipulation of the public psyche, designed to hoodwink unsuspecting citizens through an unpardonable exploitation of temporary economic pain.

Atiku’s vacillation stands as a monument to a fading presidential ambition gone completely awry, exposing a man willing to burn down national economic stability for a fleeting headline.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

A Chronicle of Political Duplicity

Let us refresh the collective memory of the Nigerian electorate, which Atiku so cynically presumes to be short. During the intense build-up to the 2023 general election, Atiku made the total removal of the fuel subsidy the absolute cornerstone of his economic manifesto.

He argued with unyielding conviction — repeatedly echoed across national media platforms, including broad coverage by outlets like Premium Times and The PUNCH — that the opaque, corruption-ridden import subsidy regime was bleeding the nation dry, enriching a parasitic cabal, and mortgaging the future of generations unborn.

Yet, as the political calendar ticks toward the next electoral cycle and the reality of his diminished prospects sets in, Atiku has engineered a shameless volte-face. The architect of yesterday’s fiscal discipline has overnight transformed into the high priest of populist pandering.

This radical reversal is the ultimate hallmark of a desperate politician who cares less about long-term fiscal sustainability and more about capturing power by any means necessary. It is a cynical bet that Nigerians have forgotten his own economic doctrine — a scorched-earth strategy that weaponises current hardships against the very structural reforms he once championed.

The Desperation of a Fading Ambition

Atiku’s career has long been shadowed by the relentless pursuit of the elusive presidency, an ambition that has increasingly degenerated into a reflex of contrarian posturing. When an administration undertakes the tortuous, necessary surgery of dismantling an unsustainable subsidy regime — a framework legally sealed by the Petroleum Industry Act — it inevitably invites short-term adjustment pains.

Rather than offering statesmanlike support or constructive alternatives, Atiku has chosen the path of political opportunism. His visible annoyance at the ongoing recovery across various sectors of our national life is telling.

The emergence of domestic refining capacity, the liberation of trillions of naira into the Federation Account for sub-national infrastructural development, and the steady weaning of the Nigerian economy from life-support leakages are milestones that threaten his political narrative. By promising to roll back these hard-won gains, Atiku reveals a transactional worldview: if he cannot rule, he would rather preside over ruins.

A Sordid Rebuttal to Economic Regression

To entertain Atiku’s hollow promise is to invite national economic suicide. The old import subsidy regime was not merely a pricing mechanism; it was a black hole of rent-seeking, round-tripping, and monumental corruption that starved health, education, and infrastructure of vital capital.

Restoring it would instantly sabotage the nascent renaissance of local refining, crush private sector confidence, and plunge the country back into chronic foreign exchange haemorrhage. Nigerians must reject this sordid narrative of regression.

True leadership requires the courage to defend difficult, foundational reforms even when the political weather is rough, rather than pandering to populist illusions for ballot-box validation.

Atiku’s hypocrisy is an insult to the collective intelligence of a resilient populace navigating global economic headwinds. By the Grace of God, this desperate gambit will fail, and all citizens of conscience must rise up to soundly repudiate this political innuendo.

Sunday Dare is the Special Adviser to the President on Media and Public Communications.

World.title: EXCLUSIVE: How Nigeria’s new ‘fake’ agency built nationwide network, sought state funds, land, more
World.content:
On Friday, the Nigerian government flagged another “fake” agency, with President Bola Tinubu suspending three top officials identified as enablers and ordering the arrest of the frontrunner.

This makes the fourth phoney agency that the Independent Corrupt Practices and Related Offences Commission (ICPC) has uncovered in its just-concluded 30-day investigation, which it submitted to Mr Tinubu.

The new agency- National Brands Development and Made in Nigeria Special Project Office- was uncovered by the ICPC barely two months after a similar case made headlines, ensnaring senior government officials, including the Chief of Staff to the President, Femi Gbajabiamila.

The agency allegedly operates under the Office of the Secretary to the Government of the Federation (OSGF), the ICPC chairperson, Musa Aliyu, told journalists after meeting with Mr Tinubu

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The discovery came amid the ICPC’s investigation into the earlier case. Although the commission said the organisation operated without presidential authorisation, documents exclusively obtained by PREMIUM TIMES show that it presented itself to state governments as an official federal initiative operating from the OSGF.

Among the documents bearing the insignia of the presidency were a letter of appointment, approvals, and a series of correspondence to state governors, seeking financial, land, and other forms of support. Aside from this, the agency has a dedicated website and state coordinators across the country, including the Federal Capital Territory (FCT).

Between January and February, it wrote to governors in Lagos, Imo, Ondo, Sokoto, Edo and Nasarawa, seeking government support, state coordinators, funding or fee, land and participation in programmes in Nigeria and abroad.

All the letters were signed by Nwabueze George, the promoter of the agency, whom Mr Tinubu ordered to be arrested immediately. In the letters, Mr George was identified as the Executive Director of the National Coordinator, Made in Nigeria Project.

The ‘Presidency’ office that governors interacted with

The agency repeatedly identified itself as a federal initiative operating from the OSGF office.

Its letters were headed “The Presidency – National Brands Development and Made in Nigeria Special Project Office” and identified the office as being under the OSGF, Director SGF Office, at Shagari House, Three Arms Zone, Abuja.

In a 9 January letter marked “Third Reminder” and addressed to Lagos State Governor Babajide Sanwo-Olu, the agency sought the nomination and appointment of a Lagos State coordinator for its purported Made in Nigeria project.

The letter said the appointment would facilitate collaboration between the federal and state governments and promote local production, small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), industrial growth and international trade.

The letter told the governor that the nominee’s details would be used for “formal confirmation” and the issuance of an appointment letter from the Abuja office.

Letter addressed to Edo provided bank accounts for payment

In one of the letters dated 23 February, the agency sought authorisation to pay for a summit in Bahrain.

The letter directed the state to make payments into accounts belonging to the Made in Nigeria Project Office, Abuja.

It provided both a naira account and a dollar domiciliary account at Zenith Bank.

The agency said it was awaiting payment of $2,500 per person for registration, exhibition and participation in the Bahrain engagement.

It proposed a quota of five government officials and 25 private-sector participants from Edo State.

At the stated rate, a full delegation of 30 people would have amounted to $75,000, equivalent to about N100 million at the estimated exchange rate at the time.

A correspondence to the Nasarawa government

The agency’s correspondence with Nasarawa State provides a clearer picture of the scale of its operation.

It sought Governor Abdullahi Sule’s support for a “national stakeholders’” meeting in Lafia, scheduled for 28 to 30 April.

The proposed meeting was to involve national coordinating officers and state coordinators and, among other objectives, to inaugurate a State Coordinators Executive Council comprising representatives from the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory.

The organisation said the event would formally launch its national structure.

Demanding a land, more financial support

The agency also sought a physical presence in Ondo State.

On 13 January, it wrote to the state governor, Lucky Aiyedatiwa, requesting land for a “Made in Nigeria Product Market.”

The proposed facility was described as a national platform for promoting, producing, exhibiting and commercialising Nigerian-made goods, brands and services.

The agency said the facility would provide space for manufacturers, artisans, innovators and SMEs and serve as a reference hub for Made in Nigeria products.

It also assured the governor that the project would comply with the Ondo Master Plan and relevant state regulations.

In another letter dated 23 January, the agency invited the Imo State Governor, Hope Uzodimma, as a “special guest of honour” and a speaker at its national inaugural convention scheduled to hold between 5 and 7 February in Lafia, Nasarawa.

The letter went beyond an invitation, asking the governor to provide financial support for transportation, hotel accommodation, feeding, conference materials, registration, training and other logistics.

The agency subsequently invited states to participate in international product fairs in Burundi, Equatorial Guinea, China, South Korea and Oman.

In a 10 February letter to Governor Ahmad Aliyu, the organisation invited Sokoto State to participate in food and agricultural expos in Bahrain and Azerbaijan.

Noting that it operates under OSGF, it wrote that it had a mandate to promote non-oil exports, showcase Nigerian agriculture and attract foreign investment.

The Bahrain event was scheduled for 1 to 5 April, while the Azerbaijan event was scheduled for 5 to 8 May.

The organisation promised participating states access to international markets, meetings with buyers and investors, and exposure to export standards and agricultural technologies.

World.title: Call me Tony: A parable of corporate Nigeria, By Temitope Lakisokun
World.content:
The awkwardness lies in the system itself: a borrowed convention that was designed to soften hierarchy but was never properly reconsidered as the generations changed… The lesson is not that young Nigerians must learn to fear their elders. It is that modernity does not require us to forget why certain social conventions existed in the first place. We are not “oyinbo.”.. Respect can coexist with equality just as much as warmth can coexist with formality.

The argument over the young trainee who addressed UBA Chairman Tony Elumelu by his first name has become a surprisingly revealing debate about Nigerian society.

One side says she was disrespectful. The other says she did nothing wrong: UBA has a first-name culture, and she followed it.

I think both sides are looking at the wrong thing.

The question is not whether she should have said “Good morning, Tony.” It is why a convention that once seemed progressive and liberating has become so awkward when applied across generations.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The answer has something to do with second-order thinking.

First-order thinking asks: What is the immediate benefit of this change?

Second-order thinking asks: What happens because of the change? And what happens after that?

Nigeria has never been particularly good at the second question.

Consider the case of the civil servants who Murtala Mohammed dismissed in 1975. They had spent their careers in government service, accumulating little beyond their salaries and quarters, no private property, no cushion against sudden displacement. Most had no reason to steal; they worked diligently because they trusted that government would honour its side of the bargain. But when the dismissal came, many were left destitute, their years of service counting for nothing. The lesson was not lost on those who survived the purge. They saw what happened to their senior colleagues and concluded that loyalty was no protection. If government could discard them at will, they had better secure themselves while they could. They saw what loyalty had cost their predecessors and resolved that they would not suffer the same fate. That was the day Nigeria’s corruption problem found its institutional footing. A straight line runs from that moment to the present.

The Great First-name Revolution

Sometime in the corporate culture of the 1980s and 1990s, a number of Nigerian executives began importing ideas from American business schools and corporate America, most of them fresh from a three- or four-week course at Harvard or Yale, which, by a happy coincidence, was just enough time to be thoroughly convinced of everything!

Among the ideas that arrived was the notion that hierarchy should be softened by having people call one another by their first names.

It made sense at the time.

Nigeria’s corporate culture could be excessively deferential. The distance between Oga and subordinate made honest conversation difficult. Junior employees might hesitate to challenge senior executives. A first-name culture promised to make the workplace less intimidating.

For a time, it worked. Most executives were peers in age and experience. Calling the managing director “Tony” or “Fola,” did not erase hierarchy; everyone still knew who held what position. The informality simply sat on top of an already understood structure. Everyone felt a little more modern, and y’know, more “with it.” This was the early ‘90s version of performative modernity.

The trouble began when time did what time always does.

The contemporaries became elders.

Then their children joined the organisations.

Now, their grandchildren are arriving as graduate trainees and interns.

It’s safe to say the old convention has encountered a circumstance its original architects had not really considered.

Imagine a chairman in his mid-to-late sixties addressing a room of young trainees. Some of them are young enough to be his grandchildren. The corporate rule says: “Call me Tony.”

The society outside the office says: “This is your elder.” So, which instruction is the young person supposed to follow?

That is the real problem and the fence nobody asked about.

GK Chesterton’s famous argument about the fence is useful here.

If you encounter a fence in the middle of a road and cannot see why it is there, the sensible response is not immediately to tear it down. First ask why someone put it there. Perhaps the fence is unnecessary. Perhaps it is protecting something you cannot see. Either way, you need to understand its purpose before removing it.

Social conventions are often like that.

A title may appear unnecessarily formal, but such conventions often perform a social function that becomes invisible, precisely because they have worked for so long.

This, in my opinion, is what the Nigerian corporate first-name revolution failed to consider. It borrowed the visible feature of another culture without necessarily considering the social system around it.

America’s informal corporate culture did not develop in a vacuum. It sits within a particular history of individualism, social mobility, and attitudes toward authority.

For centuries, Nigerian societies have attached meaning to age, seniority, office, lineage and relationship. The language of respect was one of the ways society organised itself.

A younger person knew how to address or greet an elder. A subject knew how to address a king. A junior knew how to address a senior. An apprentice knew how to address a master.

These distinctions did not necessarily mean that one human being was worth more than another. What they did was establish relationship. Unfortunately, relationship is the thing the first-name convention can obscure.

Respect Is Not the Same thing as Servility

There is an understandable desire among younger Nigerians to reject the old culture of Oga and Madam, particularly when those titles are used to demand obedience, rather than to acknowledge legitimate authority. That criticism is fair because respect should never become a licence for humiliation. But the answer to excessive deference is not necessarily the elimination of every marker of seniority.

The French still distinguish between “tu” and “vous.” Japanese language has “san” and a much wider system of honorific speech. These societies have modern economies, sophisticated corporations and highly educated young people. They have not concluded that acknowledging social distance is incompatible with modernity.

But here in Nigeria?!

Social hierarchy must disappear because “we woke.”

If UBA’s established culture is that employees call one another by their first names, then it is difficult to pile on the young lady. She may have done exactly what the institution taught her to do.

And that is precisely why the incident is more revealing than a simple story about an impolite young Nigerian.

The institution created the convention, which the employee followed.

The convention then produced a result that many people instinctively felt was wrong. Should that not make us examine the convention, rather than simply blame the individual?

The original intention may have been useful in reducing unnecessary distance between people. But second-order thinking asks what happens when that convention is carried forward for thirty years.

A policy designed by contemporaries for contemporaries has now encountered a new generation, and a well-intentioned corporate convention has become an albatross.

The Deeper Nigerian Problem

This is not really an argument for returning to an age of rigid hierarchy.

It is an argument for thinking before we dismantle things.

Nigeria has a habit of importing institutional ideas because they appear modern, without asking what assumptions make them work in their original setting. We inherit the form without understanding the function. A whole lot of, (ahem) religious practices come to mind here.

This is what Chesterton’s fence is about.

Before removing an old convention, ask what it was doing. Before telling every Nigerian employee to call every senior person by his or her first name, ask one very simple question:

What happens when the chairman is old enough to be the intern’s grandfather?

That question should have been asked thirty odd years ago.

The awkwardness lies in the system itself: a borrowed convention that was designed to soften hierarchy but was never properly reconsidered as the generations changed.

The lesson is not that young Nigerians must learn to fear their elders. It is that modernity does not require us to forget why certain social conventions existed in the first place. We are not “oyinbo.”

Respect can coexist with equality just as much as warmth can coexist with formality.

And perhaps the next time we encounter a Nigerian convention that seems old-fashioned, we should resist the reflex to tear it down simply because someone in Boston, Palo Alto or at Harvard Business School does things differently.

First ask:

Why was the fence built?

Temitope Lakisokun, a political consultant, and Chair of Trustees of the Tarihi Trust Foundation, writes from Lagos.

World.title: Hope for cancer patients as scientists report breakthrough in personalised cancer vaccines
World.content:
Researchers in the United States have reported promising results from a personalised cancer vaccine designed to prevent melanoma from returning or spreading.

The vaccine, known as intismeran autogene, is being developed by Moderna, a biotechnology company, in partnership with Merck, a biopharmaceutical company.

It is designed for patients with high-risk melanoma after their tumours have been surgically removed, Reuters reported.

According to the National Cancer Institute (NCI), melanoma is less common than other major types of skin cancer but is more likely to invade nearby tissue and spread to other parts of the body. Most deaths from skin cancer are caused by melanoma.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

The American Cancer Society estimates roughly 112,000 new cases of invasive melanoma and 8,510 deaths for 2026.

Merck and Moderna said the vaccine helped prevent the return and spread of melanoma in a large trial involving more than 1,000 patients. The patients had localised tumours that had been surgically removed but were considered to have a high risk of recurrence.

More about the vaccine

The treatment combines a personalised mRNA vaccine with Merck’s immunotherapy drug, Keytruda.

Unlike chemotherapy, which kills both healthy and cancerous cells, personalised cancer vaccines are designed to train the immune system to target mutations specific to a person’s tumour, Reuters reported.

The treatment uses up to nine doses of Keytruda, given every six weeks, together with up to nine doses of a customised mRNA vaccine. The vaccine is designed based on the specific mutations in a patient’s tumour and instructs the immune system to attack the patient’s cancer cells.

Merck describes intismeran autogene as an “mRNA-based individualised neoantigen therapy” designed around the unique mutational signature of a patient’s tumour. The company said it uses synthetic mRNA coding for up to 34 neoantigens.

Neoantigens are features of cancer cells that can help the immune system recognise and attack them.

What the trial found

Merck and Moderna said earlier five-year data from a Phase 2b trial showed that adding intismeran autogene to Keytruda reduced the risk of cancer returning or death by 49 per cent, compared with Keytruda alone.

The combination also reduced the risk of the cancer spreading to distant parts of the body or death by 59 per cent, according to Merck.

Ryan Sullivan, director of the Centre for Melanoma at Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, described the findings as “a big deal for the field in general.”

“With this positive study, there is hope,” Sullivan told Reuters, adding that the approach could change the way cancer is treated more broadly.

The Chief Medical Officer of the American Society of Clinical Oncology, Julie Gralow, described the trial results as “a monumental leap forward,” saying they validate mRNA technology as a cancer treatment.

Elizabeth Buchbinder, a melanoma specialist at the Mass General Brigham Cancer Institute, said melanoma was chosen for testing partly because it produces many mutations, making it easier for the immune system to identify.

Buchbinder said many other cancer types also produce multiple mutations, suggesting the approach could have broad applications.

“We’ll see, but it’s definitely an ​area that is going to be exploding, especially with these results coming out,” she was quoted as saying.

More cancers being studied

The research is already moving beyond melanoma. Reuters reports that Moderna and Merck are conducting trials of the treatment in other cancers, including non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer and kidney cancer.

The companies are also studying the approach in pancreatic and stomach cancers, with results from several trials expected over the next one to two years, Moderna President Stephen Hoge told Reuters.

Other companies are also developing similar mRNA cancer vaccines. Roche and BioNTech are testing a similar treatment, known as autogene cevumeran, in patients with colon and pancreatic cancers who have undergone surgery.

“We should be hearing results from multiple studies over the next few years, and there’s every reason to hope now,” Robert Vonderheide, president-elect of the American Association for Cancer Research, said.

However, the current melanoma trial is still ongoing, and the companies have not released the full results. Researchers will continue to follow participants to determine whether the treatment also extends overall survival.

In January, PREMIUM TIMES reported that Spanish scientists had eliminated pancreatic cancer tumours in laboratory mice using a combination of three drugs.

The researchers, however, stressed that the treatment had not yet been tested in humans and that further validation and safety testing would be required before human trials.

World.title: 2027: Nwifuru will defeat opposition, says Nwebonyi
World.content:
Gov Nwifuru

By Jeff Agbodo, Abakaliki

ABAKALIKI — The Deputy Chief Whip of the Senate and Senator representing Ebonyi North Senatorial District, Peter Onyekachi Nwebonyi, has declared that no opposition party can defeat Ebonyi State Governor, Francis Ogbonna Nwifuru, in the 2027 governorship election.

Nwebonyi attributed the governor’s growing political support to his administration’s achievements in infrastructure and human capital development, saying the projects would boost his chances of securing re-election.

The senator spoke at his polling unit at Community Primary School, Mbeke Ishieke, in Ebonyi Local Government Area of the state, after the local government elections.

Nwebonyi, who said he had visited about five polling units, described the voter turnout as encouraging and said it reflected growing support for the ruling All Progressives Congress (APC) in the state.

“For the last turnout in this election, I have visited about five polling units and the turnout is encouraging.

“The turnout is suggesting that Ebonyi State is APC and APC is Ebonyi State. The reason behind this turnout is not far-fetched. It is because the Governor of Ebonyi State, Rt. Hon. Francis Ogbonna Nwifuru, has put smiles on the faces of every Ebonyi person.

“That is why every Ebonyi person today is singing APC, APC, APC,” he said.

The senator said Nwifuru’s performance had strengthened his political standing ahead of the 2027 election, urging anyone planning to challenge the governor to reconsider the ambition.

“You can see a purposeful leader. You can see a man who is working for tomorrow. You can see a man with foresight. You can see a man who wants to leave Ebonyi State better than the one he is presiding over today.

“Therefore, anybody who is coming to challenge my governor in the next election is embarking on what we call a wild goose chase,” he said.

Nwebonyi particularly commended Nwifuru’s human capital development initiatives, saying the administration had provided opportunities for Ebonyi indigenes to pursue advanced education, including specialised programmes outside the country.

He also praised President Bola Tinubu, saying the administration’s infrastructure projects and federal road interventions had given people in the South-East greater confidence in the APC.

According to him, ongoing federal road projects linking the South-East with other parts of the country would improve economic integration and create new opportunities for commerce and development.

“The President and Commander-in-Chief, President Bola Ahmed Tinubu, has given the Igbo race, not just Ebonyi people, reasons to believe in APC.

“This is the first time the Federal Government is remembering significantly the people of Ebonyi State and the South-East and South-South geopolitical zones through projects of this magnitude,” he said.

Nwebonyi described the ongoing Calabar-Ebonyi-Benue-Nasarawa-Abuja highway project as a major economic corridor that would enhance connectivity among the affected states.

He said the project would facilitate the movement of people and goods while stimulating economic activities along the corridor.

The lawmaker also commended the Minister of Works, Senator David Umahi, for what he described as innovations in road construction, particularly the adoption of concrete pavement technology on major federal highways.

“While we commend the President, we must also appreciate the man I have described as a grandfather of modern Ebonyi State, His Excellency, Engineer Senator David Nweze Umahi, the immediate past governor of Ebonyi State and the current Minister of Works.

“For the wonderful innovation, you must give it to him. If you don’t like his face, please like what he is doing. You may not like him as a person, but you must appreciate the quality of work he is doing,” he said.

Nwebonyi said his support for the APC leadership at the federal and state levels was based on what he described as tangible development projects rather than political sentiment.

“Leadership is not rhetoric. Leadership is putting on the ground life-impacting projects that even the unborn generation will come and see,” he said.

The senator also highlighted some of his constituency projects, including road construction, educational support, scholarships, street lighting and market development.

He said more than 900 students from Ebonyi North and other areas had benefited from his scholarship programme, while several infrastructure projects were ongoing across communities in the senatorial district.

Nwebonyi said the development of a regional market along the new highway corridor would boost agricultural trade and provide farmers and traders with access to wider markets.

“This site building will serve as a prototype of what is going to be here,” he said, adding that the project was expected to be completed by December.

He said the market, when completed, would complement the area’s strategic position as a commercial and agricultural hub.

Nwebonyi further said governance should be driven by sacrifice and a commitment to improving citizens’ lives.

“A leader should be ready to spend all he has. A leader should be ready to spend whatever comes his way, including his personal income, to help the people. That is leadership,” he said.

He urged political leaders and Nigerians to support public office holders who demonstrate commitment to development irrespective of political differences.

“If somebody is doing well, commend him. President Tinubu is doing well. The Minister of Works is doing well. My governor is doing well,” Nwebonyi said.

World.title: Oil Crisis: FG not under obligation to solve all Ogoni problems – MOSOP
World.content:
By Daniel Abia

P/Harcourt

Movement for the Survival of the Ogoni People, MOSOP, has expressed support for the on-going dialogue between the Ogoni people and the Federal Government, describing its support base as overwhelming and irrevocable.

MOSOP says the organization’s commitment to see a permanent resolution to the Ogoni problem is firm, strong and intense, adding that though government may not be under obligation to resolve all the problems confronting Ogoniland, “we stand to benefit substantially from the ongoing dialogue”.

MOSOP President, Fegalo Nsuke, who spoke during an interview with journalists in Port Harcourt on Sunday said the collective interest of the Ogoni people “far outweighs personal interests” and urged the Ogoni public to reject manipulative and misleading information designed to frustrate the goodwill of the Federal Government.

Nsuke said the expectation of MOSOP was not to get the federal government to solve all Ogoni problems, saying that getting the federal government to make the necessary compromises that allows the Ogoni people to design and structure an Ogoni-centric system that provides the environment to deal with critical issues affecting the future of the Ogoni people including job creation, security, health, infrastructure, education, electricity and so on.

“We do not need to be asking the government for jobs; we need to have a system that creates the jobs, and that is the goal of the ongoing dialogue. We need a system that addresses our social problems including job creation, health, education, electricity and so on, and not running to the government with all our problems in search of solutions. This dialogue will try to get the necessary concessions that enable Ogoni to develop its resources and get the right benefits from them,” Nsuke said.

He stated unequivocally that MOSOP is fully mobilized to support the dialogue process and urged the Ogoni people not to forget yesterday and how self-seeking disagreements have hurt the collective efforts of the people to make progress. He further noted that external influences were misinforming the Ogoni public to frustrate the Ogoni people’s efforts to achieve a better life.

“We cannot continue to grapple with poverty and unemployment when the land we walk on every day has the capacity to generate over $50million daily. Anyone deceiving us into protesting against current dialogue does not mean well.”

“I can tell you that the government has not shown any signs of mistrust, and the dialogue process is currently going well. The dialogue committee has submitted a fine report, and the next phase is to see how best we can negotiate a good deal for the people.”

“We must remain focused on the common good and not fall for cheap blackmail and manipulations. What is most important for our people at this time is to guide the ongoing dialogue process and ensure that we make the best use of it.”

“Let us not forget that it has taken us over 33 years to come this far. Being deceived to fight the process will be the most unpatriotic thing to do at this time, especially because it has not been easy to initiate the ongoing dialogue process”

Nsuke urged Ogoni to be wise, accusing external enemies and Non-Governmental Organizations (NGOs) whose survival sdepends on the sufferings and struggles of the Ogoni people of ganging up against the dialogue to prolong the Ogoni conflicts.

“I want to call on everyone to give the Ogoni people the chance to resolve our problems ourselves. I am unfortunately very disappointed that people who have not questioned oil drilling in their locality are discouraging Ogoni people from dialoguing with the Federal Government”.

“No one should deceive you to think that there is a better alternative to dialogue. We should be grateful to the current government, who have found it necessary to open discussions with us.”

“This is a fine opportunity, and people who have benefitted from our sufferings and deprivations should not deceive us into endless resistance. We must continue to engage and protect current dialogue because it is one good opportunity before us,” Nsuke concluded.

World.title: Olu of Warri’s fifth Anniversary: It’s about culture, homecoming, empowerment – Lawrence Wilbert
World.content:
As the Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse III, marks his fifth year on the throne, activities are being held across the kingdom to celebrate the anniversary and promote the culture, identity and development of the Itsekiri people.



In this interview, the Agura Tete of Warri Kingdom, Chief Lawrence Wilbert, speaks on the significance of the anniversary, the Olu’s vision for Warri Kingdom, the preservation of Itsekiri language and culture, inter-ethnic relations in the Niger Delta, and the potential of Warri as a hub for blue economy.

By Charles Kumolu, Deputy Editor



The Olu of Warri, Ogiame Atuwatse lll, is celebrating his fifth year on the throne…



The formal programme started on August 17, with activities highlighting what Ogiame has been able to achieve this year with the Global Homecoming of Itsekiri people.



That was preceded by an Itsekiri language competition involving children, which is part of the efforts to promote the language among the younger generation.



There were also a series of activities taking place across the kingdom before the formal programme. One of these is the Benin River Life series of events, which takes place on August 15. There are also activities involving gospel artistes and other programmes.



There was also a novelty football match on August 20.

What does the fifth coronation anniversary mean to the Itsekiri people?



The king lives forever. Five years is a landmark, and His Majesty, Ogiame Atuwatse III, is someone who makes sure that his family, his children and his subjects are involved in everything that will bring life and progress to them.



For the fifth coronation anniversary, he considered it an opportunity for Itsekiri people all over the world to return home. It is not limited to Itsekiri alone. It includes friends of Itsekiri and everyone who has blood ties to Itsekiri.

His Majesty is looking forward to personally welcoming them and participating in events with them. It has so far been a grand occasion.



The anniversary provides an opportunity to say that, after five years of building, this is the time to come together once again and celebrate as a people.



We have a history and a traditional institution that goes back more than 500 years. That heritage cannot simply be written away. There was a period when people lost confidence in who they were, but today, the Itsekiri are becoming increasingly confident in their identity, particularly with a king like Ogiame Atuwatse III on the throne.The future is bright.

Beyond culture and tradition, what would you say has been the major focus of the Olu in the last five years?

I am not talking only about culture and tradition only. I am talking about the livelihood of the ordinary Itsekiri person.



For at least the past two years, His Majesty has focused increasingly on what is happening to his people economically. We are a people who sit on the wealth that feeds Nigeria from an economic perspective, particularly through the oil and gas industry, yet we remain among the poorest.

His Majesty has been addressing that reality.



Thankfully, the Petroleum Industry Act has also been implemented over these years. Beyond that, His Majesty has focused on cultural diplomacy, engaging not only the ethnic nationalities around us and across Nigeria, but also traditional institutions and ethnic nationalities in different parts of Africa.



He is part of a broader conversation about the renaissance of African identity and the recognition of the leadership role Africa should play in the world.



For the Itsekiri, it is exciting to be part of that process. Africa is coming into its own, and His Majesty has been working towards that. I think this fifth coronation anniversary is an opportunity to bring all those efforts together and showcase that we are a humble people, but we know who we are and we are ready for the world.

A few years ago, the Olu instituted awards such as the Royal Order of Iwere, ROl, What special activities or initiatives should people expect during this anniversary?



His Majesty has the prerogative to determine what he wants to present and showcase to the rest of the world.



But what is important is that we want to demonstrate that all the work that has been done in human capacity development and the repositioning of Warri Kingdom is beginning to bear fruit.

Those who have previously received awards are now demonstrating their impact. The Itsekiri Global Homecoming, for example, is being championed by recipients of the Royal Order of Iwere.



This is the first time something like this is happening, and they have taken it upon themselves to make sure that it happens.



We are also going to have royal representatives from different parts of Africa.

You will see the richness and diversity of Itsekiri communities, whether they are poor or wealthy. We are talking about the Benin River axis and the culture that exists there. The camaraderie and even the friendly rivalry among the communities will all manifest through the Benin River Life series of events.

The Minister of Culture, Arts and Tourism will be present and is very excited about the programme. The Minister of Communications will also be involved. There is an opportunity to work with the Iwere Kingdom to explore how telecommunications and communications infrastructure can be expanded in the riverine areas.



So, the impact of His Majesty’s reach, words and actions is gradually coming into manifestation.

The Itsekiri Kingdom is located in an area where there have been concerns about inter-ethnic relations. To what extent is the Olu addressing these challenges?



These situations exist, but the beauty about the king we have is that he is at the forefront of addressing them. He does not take the back seat. He is involved in the key decisions and in determining how things should be driven.



Interestingly, the main players in the area, the Itsekiri, Ijaw and Urhobo, have a very high level of mixed marriages. You cannot even define it.



When you begin to look at issues around land and political territories, however, there is something else at play. It is power.

What is important is that we engage at all levels and have a conversation that says what belongs to you should be yours. At the same time, we must recognise historical realities and understand that these things have always existed. There is no need to fight over them.



The Warri axis, including the Warri Kingdom and neighbouring kingdoms, has been brought to its knees by ethnic nationality strife.

There are also new players in the game who are making wealth from these divisions.



The rule should be simple: if I have a glass house, I will not throw stones at your glass house because you will throw them back.



I am happy for the wealth that is being created among everybody. At that point, there is nobody with sovereign power over violence. If the Urhobo are violent, if the Ijaw are violent and if the Itsekiri are violent, who pays the price? All of us will pay the price, because when there is violence, nobody makes money.



Stability is important. Everybody should be able to make money and develop.



Above all, there is a sovereign God who sees everything.

The Itsekiri are known for their rich cultural heritage. What has sustained the culture over the centuries?

That is a very interesting question.



The simple answer is: water no get enemy.



His Majesty has spoken about this philosophy before. He is not merely planning for the next cycle or even the next generation. He is laying institutional foundations for the next seven generations.



He views leadership through the water cycle. Water flows. It does not get in anybody’s way. It nourishes, replenishes and empowers communities.



The Itsekiri person is very close to water. We are a water people.



If you observe our dances, particularly the way the women dance, there is a certain grace to it. It is like the movement of a duck on water. Even when there is a storm underneath, what you see is the graceful movement on the surface.



When you see the men dancing, it can also look as if they are swimming.



That is the gracious movement and respect for water, and it translates into many aspects of Itsekiri life and culture.

One of the anniversary programmes focuses on the Itsekiri language. There have been concerns that the language could eventually become endangered. Do you share those concerns?



Itsekiri is a minority ethnic nationality, and in Nigeria, the three major ethnic nationalities have their languages promoted extensively.



If intentional action is not taken to protect minority languages, they will go into extinction.

And this is not only an Itsekiri problem. It applies to many minority ethnic nationalities.



If you travel across Nigeria, you hear the names of ethnic groups and their languages, many of which you may never have heard of before.



We are fortunate as Itsekiri to have the visibility that we have. There are other ethnic nationalities with populations similar to ours that do not have that level of visibility.



One thing the Itsekiri must do is to be intentional about preserving the language.



That is why His Majesty has put the issue at the forefront. He is personally involved in celebrating children who are proficient in the language.



But much more needs to be done.



We need teacher training in the language. We need scholarships for people who want to become Itsekiri language teachers. We need to create jobs for them in our primary and secondary schools and, for those who are qualified, at the tertiary level.



We also need researchers and fellows working on the language. We should create faculties or academic chairs dedicated to Itsekiri studies so that there can be further research and development of the language.



It is a rich language. For a people with a history of more than 500 years, it is only logical that we should intentionally do more to preserve it for another 500 years and beyond.

Warri is almost as famous as Nigeria itself, but the city still has significant infrastructure challenges. To what extent is the Olu pushing for the development and renewal of Warri?



Warri was one of the early points of contact with the Portuguese. In the ancestral home of the Itsekiri, you also have what is believed to be one of the earliest Catholic churches in Nigeria, St Anthony’s Catholic Church, known locally as Satoni.



We also have a long history of engagement with Europe and an ethnic nationality that produced what is arguably one of the earliest European-educated monarchs in West Africa, Dom Domingo.



So, we have come a long way, even before the emergence of Nigeria. We are a nation, and we predate Nigeria, just as other great kingdoms, including the Benin Kingdom from which our monarch’s lineage comes, predate the modern Nigerian state.



Now, moving to Warri as it is today, much of what you see is a consequence of the ethnic strife that has affected the city and its environs.



We must commend the leadership of Governor Sheriff Oborevwori for helping to calm the situation that arose recently.



What Warri needs most is peace among its peoples.



Warri will always be a magnet for investment, particularly in the oil and gas sector.



But there is another opportunity that we do not talk about enough: the blue economy.



Warri has the potential to become a major hub for the blue economy, not just through industries that will operate there, but also through the development of human capital that can be exported from the entire Niger Delta region.



Look at the Philippines. It is a major player in the maritime sector partly because it exports its citizens as human capital. You go to ships around the world and you find Filipinos.



The Philippines does not have as large a population as Nigeria. It also has a coastline, just as Nigeria does. Yet Nigeria is not even doing five per cent of what the Philippines is doing in terms of exporting maritime human capital.



Warri therefore has enormous potentialities. What we need is peace, stability, investment and deliberate development of the people and institutions that can turn that potential into wealth.

Bight of Benin



We are poor, but in reality, we are rich with our human resources. What can be done around the blue economy? When I say Warri, I am actually talking about Warri Kingdom, because you have a long stretch of ocean that goes across the Bight of Benin, and you have the various ethnic nationalities that are conversant with the creeks and those waters. There is a lot that can be done from that perspective.



Now, to His Majesty, he sees the future of what we collectively, as a people, can make our homestead become. We can make it the greatest of all, because we have everything within us, both human and natural resources, to make all that happen.



From that perspective, His Majesty engages his brother kings. It is from that perspective you see him engaging not just the local government authorities, but the state government authorities, the national and federal authorities, and, of course, with the permission of the Federal Government, you see him engaging even in cultural diplomacy with the rest of Africa and the rest of the world.



All this is to bring attention to the potentialities in this area we call Warri Kingdom, which is not just Warri Kingdom itself, but even its environment and its neighbours, and to see what can be attracted to it.

Cultural diplomacy



You can see His Majesty undertaking a cultural diplomacy trip to Finland, because Finland is a forerunner in the education sector, where they have one of the most educated societies in the world. We want to learn from them.



His Majesty wants to learn from them. He needs his people to be better educated. What have they done there that we can imbibe?



You have His Majesty engaging with His Majesty in the United Kingdom, King Charles, to maintain those relationships. You have His Majesty undertaking trips to Canada and even to the United States, all this to engage technocrats and see history. We are blessed with our culture, which has gone on for so long.



We are blessed currently with a visionary king, one who has a heart for his people. The ingredient needed right now is the belief or the execution of His Majesty’s vision for the Kingdom. The commitment to want to see that this Kingdom carries on being here for another 500 years by participating.



And that is what His Majesty is trying to underline, even with this fifth coronation anniversary, by calling his children to come home and see your lands, see how beautiful it is. It has challenges, but the land needs you right now. That commitment from every son and daughter.



The other ingredient that the Itsekiri need now is to see that their destiny is right in their hands. Nobody else can execute what they aspire for, which is good livelihood, peaceful living, the ability to express themselves, to acquire happiness, to have jobs and maintain an environment that is sustainable. Now, it is in their hands.

It will also include a change in work ethic, which His Majesty is preaching, from a rent-seeking attitude to being a productive people, because our land is now, “Walk the land, work the land, bring out what you need.”



We have seen your transition from the corporate sector to a notable titled person. Can you tell us what it feels like playing this role, and what are those responsibilities that the position placed or places on you?

I would want to address that by starting off by saying Ogiame, I suppose, did not confer the title and the responsibility on me to come and just sit and wear the title as a chief. He knew and knows that I’m a technocrat.



He knew and knows that I’m a leader. He knew and knows that I’m one that connects the nation. Interestingly, my Akuja, the appellation which he blessed me with, is Ajolaja, Ajolaja, the repairer of the town, the unifier, the one who makes things happen.

Now, I am a chief of the Ogiame Court, with leadership amongst the chiefs. We are blessed to have the leadership of Chief Oma, who is the Ologbotsere of Warri Kingdom, who himself, yes, is aged, but a brilliant first-class technocrat. He is a first-class graduate, a technocrat, an engineer.



He is a great leader to have on the chieftaincy train. Mine is to see how I add my own flair to the expression of the vision that His Majesty has laid for us.

That said, I represent Itsekiri across the whole Kingdom, but I also have a people in those states where I’m also from, which is Ikara in the Iyashere lineage. So, you find that in all that, there have been challenges for my people, the Ikara people, in where you might call the Olugbo Forest Reserve area.



There’s a lot that is going on in that angle, and thank God for Ogiame, who supports all that. Thank God for the leadership of the Iyashere of Warri Kingdom, Chief Johnson Asheruneghe, who also provides assistance to see that we can do what we need to do to get our rights done.

It has been an interesting transition from being just a pure technocrat to now being a titled chief, because every Itsekiri that sees me dressed like this, or even sees me dressed traditionally, sees Ogiame. We are a direct representation of Ogiame, so we must carry ourselves accordingly, with the grace and dignity that the office demands.

But even more so, they also demand good leadership.



Ogiame is providing that for us, so we can only just reflect that and bring our own experience to bear.

World.title: 2027: Akwa Ibom Stakeholders endorse Tinubu, Akpabio, Eno
World.content:
President Tinubu

By Henry Umoru

ABUJA — Ahead of the 2027 general elections, critical stakeholders from the Ikot Ekpene Senatorial District of Akwa Ibom State, cutting across the All Progressives Congress (APC), Peoples Democratic Party (PDP), Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) and other political groups, have endorsed the re-election bids of President Bola Tinubu, Senate President Godswill Akpabio and Governor Umo Eno.

The stakeholders announced their endorsement in a communique issued after a meeting of political leaders and other critical stakeholders from the district.

The communique was read by the member representing Ukanafun/Oruk Anam Federal Constituency, Hon. Unyime Idem, and endorsed through a voice vote following a motion moved by Senator Emmanuel Ibokessien and seconded by Hon. Iboro Ekanem.

According to a statement issued on Sunday by the Special Assistant to the President of the Senate on Media, Jackson Udom, the stakeholders reviewed the political situation in the state and assessed the contributions and performance of the three leaders before arriving at the decision.

The communique read in part: “After reviewing the political situation and assessing the contributions and performance of the leaders and representatives, the stakeholders resolved to endorse them for another term in office in the 2027 General Elections.

“Accordingly, the meeting endorsed President Bola Ahmed Tinubu for another term as President of the Federal Republic of Nigeria in the 2027 Presidential Election; Senator Godswill Obot Akpabio for another term as Senator representing Akwa Ibom North-West Senatorial District in the 2027 National Assembly Election; and Governor Umo Bassey Eno for another term as Governor of Akwa Ibom State in the 2027 Governorship Election.”

Reacting to the endorsement, Akpabio attributed the development to what he described as the peaceful atmosphere in the state and the unity among political stakeholders.

He said the endorsement demonstrated that opposition parties in the state were also supporting Tinubu’s administration.

“The peace in the state has finally led to the opposition parties joining to declare that they all stand on the mandate of Mr President,” Akpabio said.

He expressed appreciation for the endorsement, saying it showed that there was unity in Akwa Ibom State, particularly in the North-West Senatorial District.

Akpabio also assured Tinubu and Eno of the district’s support during the elections.

“I can assure President Bola Ahmed Tinubu and Governor Umo Eno that the people of this district will give them 100 percent of the votes,” he said.

The Senate President noted the presence of the Akwa Ibom State PDP Chairman, Hon. Aniekan Akpan, as well as some opposition candidates in the National Assembly elections at the meeting.

He further appealed to political actors in the state to sustain peaceful coexistence and forgive one another in the interest of the state.

“I will still continue to solicit for peaceful co-existence amongst us all. Whoever we have wronged in the course of our politicking, let us forgive and forget so that we can move in one direction and one voice during the electioneering and voting,” he said.

Former Minister of Petroleum Resources, Don Etiebet; retired Deputy Inspector-General of Police, Udom Ekpoudom; Senators Aloysius Etuk, Emmanuel Ibokessien and Chris Ekpenyong, among other stakeholders, also pledged their support for the re-election of Tinubu, Akpabio and Eno.

World.title: Tinubu’s Group to Atiku: Leave foreign interference, campaign on policies
World.content:
By Emmanuel Iheaka

The Deputy National Leader (Southeast) of the Renewed Hope for Greater Nigeria (RHGN), Mazi Clement Ngoforo, has urged former Vice President Atiku Abubakar to focus on convincing Nigerians about his plans for the country rather than seeking foreign intervention in Nigeria’s political affairs.

Ngoforo made the call shortly after the flag-off of RHGN’s campaign activities for President Bola Tinubu’s re-election in Jos, Plateau State, on Saturday.

He argued that seeking external influence in domestic political matters could portray a presidential aspirant as unwilling to face democratic competition.

According to him, any candidate seeking to govern Nigeria should focus on convincing Nigerian voters by presenting credible alternatives to the government’s approach to the country’s economic, security and developmental challenges.

“If Atiku believes Nigerians do not want Tinubu, he should go to Nigerians and persuade them. If he believes Tinubu is legally unqualified, he should make his case under Nigerian law,” Ngoforo said.

He urged Nigerians to reject political strategies that could expose the country’s electoral process to what he described as undue external influence.

Ngoforo also called on voters to support Tinubu based on what he described as the administration’s record and ongoing development agenda, while urging RHGN members and supporters to intensify grassroots mobilisation nationwide.

He said the 2027 general election should provide Nigerians with an opportunity to exercise their sovereignty by choosing their president through the country’s democratic process.

“The Nigerian President will not be elected in an American school, lobbying office or courtroom; he will be elected by Nigerians, on Nigerian soil, through the Nigerian ballot.

“If there is a question about a Nigerian election, take it to the Nigerian courts and allow Nigerian law to determine it,” Ngoforo said.

World.title: EPL: Maresca begins Man City reign with comeback win over Bournemouth
World.content:
Manchester City’s Croatian defender #24 Josko Gvardiol celebrates with teammates after a VAR (Video Assistant Referee) review clears his late goal during the English Premier League football match between Manchester City and AFC Bournemouth at the Etihad Stadium in Manchester, north west England, on August 23, 2026. (Photo by Darren Staples / AFP) / RESTRICTED TO EDITORIAL USE. No use with unauthorized audio, video, data, fixture lists, club/league logos or ‘live’ services. Online in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No video emulation. Social media in-match use limited to 120 images. An additional 40 images may be used in extra time. No use in betting publications, games or single club/league/player publications. /

Manchester City made a winning start to life without Pep Guardiola as late goals from Marc Guehi and Josko Gvardiol snatched a dramatic 2-1 victory against Bournemouth on Sunday in Enzo Maresca’s first Premier League game as the Spaniard’s replacement.

Marcus Tavernier’s first half goal put Bournemouth ahead at the Etihad Stadium before City staged a pulsating fightback in the final minutes.

Marc Guehi headed City’s equaliser with six minutes left before Gvardiol stroked in the stoppage-time winner.

Guardiola won 20 trophies, including six Premier League titles, during a glorious decade with City.

His reign started with a late win at home to Sunderland in 2016 and Maresca will hope his own narrow victory serves as the prelude to an equally successful spell.

Maresca insists he can replicate Guardiola’s trophy haul if he is given time to handle the “big changes” at the club.

City’s lacklustre 3-0 defeat against Arsenal in last weekend’s Community Shield raised questions about their ability to keep pace with the Premier League champions this season.

For much of their top-flight opener, City were again short of inspiration in attack and cohesion at the back.

But they found a way to dig out a result that allowed Maresca to breath a sigh of relief.

It is a time of major upheaval at City, with Rodri, Bernardo Silva, John Stones, Nathan Ake and Tijjani Reijnders all leaving and Savinho set to join Tottenham.

England midfielder Elliot Anderson has been Maresca’s only major signing and he was unimpressive before hobbling off in the second half.

City are set to sign teenage Morocco midfielder Ayyoub Bouaddi from Lille in a deal worth £86 million ($117 million), according to reports on Sunday.

But more new recruits will be needed if City are to close the gap on Arsenal.

– Critical decision –

Maresca wasted little time emulating one aspect of Guardiola’s reign as he unveiled a curious starting line-up.

The Italian picked six players who could be classed as defenders, with England centre-back Guehi deployed in midfield and Nico O’Reilly moved from his usual role on the left to a position closer to Erling Haaland in attack.

Haaland shed his long blond hair on the eve of the new season, describing his close-cropped look as “new season, new trim”.

The City striker, who starred for Norway at the World Cup, might have looked sharp, but his finishing was rusty when he somehow prodded wide from close-range after O’Reilly’s cross presented him with a golden opportunity.

City were punished by an incisive counter from Bournemouth in the 26th minute.

Evanilson’s perfectly weighted cross fizzed across the penalty area as City defenders Ruben Dias and Abdukodir Khusanov stood statuesque, allowing Tavernier time and space to stroke a composed finish past Gianluigi Donnarumma from six yards.

City forwards Phil Foden and Antoine Semenyo struggled to link up effectively with Haaland, whose glancing header was clawed away by Djordje Petrovic.

Guehi should have equalised immediately after the interval from Foden’s corner, but he surpassed Haaland’s woeful first half miss with an even worse header from virtually on the line.

Moans from supporters underwhelmed by Maresca’s style of play were a constant soundtrack to his time at Chelsea.

It must have alarmed City’s hierarchy to hear similar complaints from the stands before Maresca had even completed 90 minutes in charge.

But Maresca made the critical decision to send on French playmaker Rayan Cherki and the move changed the course of the match.

It was Cherki’s corner that arrowed towards Guehi in the 84th minute, presenting the defender with a chance that he headed past Petrovic in clinical fashion.

And in stoppage-time, Cherki slipped a deft pass through the heart of the Bournemouth defence for Gvardiol to slot home as Maresca punched the air in delight.

World.title: FG moves to ensure textbooks reach learners, tackles learning poverty
World.content:
By Adesina Wahab

LAGOS — The Federal Government has commenced steps to ensure that textbooks in Mathematics, English Language and other core subjects reach learners and are properly tracked and maintained as part of efforts to tackle learning poverty in Nigeria.

The initiative is being implemented through a series of workshops organised by the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) in conjunction with the Federal Ministry of Education (FME) under the Human Capital Opportunities for Prosperity and Equity (HOPE-EDU) programme.

The latest workshop, titled “Five-day Result Area One Regional Thematic Workshop on Book Supply Chain and Track ‘N’ Trace,” commenced in Lagos at the weekend.

The workshop brought together education officers from Niger, Kogi, Kwara, Nasarawa, Benue, Plateau, Ekiti, Ondo, Ogun, Osun, Oyo and Lagos states, as well as the Federal Capital Territory (FCT), Abuja.

HOPE-EDU is a Federal Government initiative supported by the World Bank to strengthen foundational learning through improved systems, institutional capacity and technical support.

Under Results Area 1 (RA1), the programme is convening a series of regional thematic workshops on the Structured Pedagogy Package (SPP) Guidance and the Book Supply Chain and Track-and-Trace (BSC/TnT) System to strengthen the capacity of federal and state officials to support effective implementation.

In her address, the Executive Secretary of UBEC, Dr Aisha Garba, commended the Federal Government and the Federal Ministry of Education for supporting the commission in implementing the HOPE-EDU programme.

Garba said the workshops were designed to translate the programme’s objectives into practical support for states by equipping relevant federal and state officials with the knowledge, tools and systems required to strengthen implementation.

She said the workshops would also demonstrate the government’s commitment to improving the quality and availability of teaching and learning materials while building transparent and accountable systems for education service delivery.

“The engagement should therefore be positioned not simply as a technical workshop, but as an important step in translating HOPE-EDU’s investments and objectives into practical improvements at state and school levels, ultimately contributing to better teaching and learning outcomes for Nigerian children,” she said.

Garba further stressed the importance of the November 15, 2026 deadline for states to demonstrate readiness for the programme.

“By November 15, 2026, your states must demonstrate readiness. This is not negotiable. It is the gateway to unlocking the first round of programme disbursements and, more importantly, the future of our children,” she said.

She noted that the participation of directors responsible for academic services, teacher professional development, monitoring and evaluation, procurement, and planning, research and statistics/electronic management information systems reflected the whole-of-system approach required for successful implementation.

In her welcome remarks, the Programme Manager, Dr Aisha Abdul, said the HOPE-EDU programme became effective in February 2026, adding that implementation had focused on establishing the institutional, technical and operational foundations required to achieve its Programme Development Objective and Year 1 results.

According to her, with the support of the World Bank team, technical experts and consultants, the programme had worked closely with states to lay the groundwork for reforms that the workshop would translate into action.

Abdul said the Book Supply Chain and Track-and-Trace System was central to the programme’s commitment to ensuring that teaching and learning materials procured and financed through HOPE-EDU achieve a 1:1 pupil-to-book ratio in literacy and numeracy and reach classrooms intact and on time.

She urged state delegations to participate actively in the workshop, resolve outstanding issues and leave with clear and actionable implementation plans.

Abdul also drew participants’ attention to the November 15 deadline for submission of prerequisite evidence, urging states to use the workshop to resolve outstanding clarifications and avoid being caught unprepared.

A representative of the Federal Ministry of Education, Mr Abdulgafar Otunola, said the ministry would continue its efforts to reposition the education sector.

A World Bank consultant, Gerard Peart, said the bank was supporting HOPE-EDU within the context of the Universal Basic Education programme.

He identified quality, access and system strengthening as critical to making primary education functional, noting that learning poverty remained a major challenge in the sector.

“One of the major problems confronting primary education in Nigeria is learning poverty occasioned by overcrowded classrooms, lack of textbooks, teaching and learning materials. If we want to get more from basic education, textbooks must be available in the classrooms and in required quantity,” Peart said.

World.title: NGE Conference: Onaiyekan, Mbah, Osigwe, others to speak in Enugu
World.content:
Cardinal John Onaiyekan

The Nigerian Guild of Editors (NGE) has announced that its 2026 All Nigeria Editors Conference (ANEC) will hold at the International Conference Centre (ICC), Enugu, on September 24 and 25.

More than 500 editors from across the country, alongside other distinguished guests, are expected at the annual conference, which is the flagship gathering of the Guild.

The 2026 edition will focus on critical national and global issues, particularly the role of the media in strengthening democracy ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The theme of the conference is “The Ballot, the Media and the Task of Keeping Democracy Alive,” while the sub-theme is “When Lies Look Real: Detecting and Debunking AI Disinformation Before, During and After Election.”

His Royal Majesty, Igwe Nnaemeka Alfred Achebe, the Obi of Onitsha, will chair the conference.

In a statement signed by the NGE President and General Secretary, Eze Anaba and Onuoha Ukeh, respectively, the Guild said the conference would provide an opportunity for media leaders and other stakeholders to examine the challenges confronting democracy and the media’s role in safeguarding credible elections, public trust and democratic values.

Former Catholic Archbishop of Abuja, Cardinal John Onaiyekan, is scheduled to deliver the keynote address at the opening ceremony on September 24 at 2pm.

Also on the first day, Prof. Auwal Yadudu of the Faculty of Law, Bayero University, Kano, will speak on “Public Trust, Electoral Justice and Democratic Stability,” while Enugu State Governor, Dr Peter Mbah, will address the conference.

Ombudsman and Public Protector of ThisDay Newspapers, Kayode Komolafe, and veteran journalist and civil rights campaigner, Owei Lakemfa, will jointly present a paper titled “Reporting Terrorism Without Becoming a Tool for Terrorists.”

The second day will feature a presentation by the immediate past President of the Nigerian Bar Association, Mazi Afam Osigwe, on “Election Petitions in the Digital Age: Independence, Evidence, BVAS and the Courts.” His presentation is scheduled for 9am.

Deputy Vice-Chancellor of Paul University, Awka, Prof. Chinyere Okunna, will speak on “Neutrality, Professionalism and Election Security in Democratic Governance.”

Founder and Chief Medical Director of Save A Life Hospital, Port Harcourt, Dr Richard Okoye, will address the issue of journalists’ welfare and wellbeing in a presentation titled “The Human Side of Journalism: Managing Stress, Deadlines and Personal Wellbeing.”

Professor of Journalism and Emerging Media at Kennesaw State University, Georgia, United States, Prof. Farooq A. Kperogi, will examine the conference’s sub-theme on detecting and debunking artificial intelligence-generated disinformation before, during and after elections.

The second day will also feature an Executive Session at 12:30pm, during which editors will engage governors, political party leaders and heads of government parastatals on issues of national importance.

The Guild said the conference would provide a platform for editors and other stakeholders to explore pathways for advancing democratic governance, promoting national development and strengthening nation-building through responsible and responsive journalism.

It added that the gathering would enable media leaders to interrogate emerging threats to democracy and develop strategies for ensuring that the media continues to play a critical role in promoting credible elections, public accountability and democratic stability.

World.title: NSE Honours Gov Sule for Engineering-Driven Development in Nasarawa
World.content:
Funmi Ogundare

The Nigerian Society of Engineers (NSE) has honoured Nasarawa State Governor, Abdullahi Sule, with its Presidential Merit award for his administration’s investments in infrastructure, engineering education, technical training and human capital development.

The National President of the NSE, Ali Rabiu, announced the award, Thursday when he led members of the society’s National Executive Committee ( NEC) on a courtesy visit to the governor at the Government House, Lafia.

He stated that the recognition followed a two-day inspection tour of major projects across the state by the NSE team, including the Mararaba twin flyovers, Diamond New Energy lithium plant in Endo, Keffi flyover, Faculty of Engineering at Nasarawa State University, Keffi, Akwanga bypass and underpass, Wing Commander Abdullahi Ibrahim Vocational and Technology Institute and Isa Mustapha Agwai I Polytechnic.

According to him, “The inspection revealed substantial and commendable investments by the Nasarawa State Government, with engineering, technical education and human capital development serving as key drivers of economic transformation.”

He said the Mararaba and Keffi flyovers were progressing satisfactorily at about 50 per cent and 70 per cent completion respectively, with generally good construction standards.

The NSE president also described the Diamond New Energy lithium plant as an important step towards local mineral processing and value addition, noting that the facility reportedly had a processing capacity of about 6,000 tonnes daily and was expected to create more than 1,000 direct and indirect jobs.

He, however, stressed the need for environmental monitoring, responsible mining practices and land reclamation around the project.

He particularly commended the Wing Commander Abdullahi Ibrahim Vocational and Technology Institute for training about 10,000 beneficiaries in various trades.

He stated: “The quality of equipment at the institute was superior to what the NSE team had seen during its inspection of engineering faculties in 12 Nigerian universities under a separate Federal Government intervention programme.”

Rabiu also commended the Isa Mustapha Agwai I Polytechnic for securing National Board for Technical Education (NBTE) accreditation for 11 new engineering programmes, while recommending improved road access within the institution.

He identified shortages of equipment, academic staff, reliable electricity and internet connectivity at the Faculty of Engineering, Nasarawa State University, Keffi, ahead of its professional accreditation, stressing the need for the university to prioritise accreditation by the Council for the Regulation of Engineering in Nigeria (COREN).

“Such accreditation is necessary to ensure graduates are eligible to practise engineering in the country,” Rabiu said, adding that the inspection had demonstrated that the state was implementing wide-ranging interventions in infrastructure, mineral processing, engineering education and vocational training.

The president recommended that the government establish a professional development and documentation framework to systematically record, communicate and preserve information on its projects and their impact.

“We therefore recommend that the state government should establish a professional development and documentation framework to systematically record, communicate and preserve information on government projects and their impacts,” he said, assuring the governor of the NSE’s readiness to strengthen its partnership with the state through professional and technical support.

Rabiu appealed to Sule to expedite the release of the Certificate of Occupancy for land previously donated to the NSE Lafia branch and provide a vehicle to support the branch’s project supervision activities across the state.

In his response, Sule thanked the NSE for selecting Nasarawa to host its NEC meeting and for the recognition, which he said was particularly significant to him because of his engineering background.

“I have received several awards, including some that I value very, very high. But I truly value an NSE golden award. That’s an award that means a lot to me,” the governor stated.

He linked his administration’s emphasis on technical and vocational education to his personal background, recalling that he trained as a certified welding technician and CNC machinist before becoming an engineer.

He said the experience influenced his investment in the Wing Commander Abdullahi Ibrahim Vocational and Technology Institute, with the ambition of replicating in Lafia the standard associated with the old Government Technical College, Bukuru.

World.title: 5th Anniversary: Warri Monarch Calls for National Unity, Cultural Renewal
World.content:
* Oborevwori hails Olu’s reign

Sylvester Idowu in Warri

The Olu of Warri, His Majesty Ogiame Atuwatse III, has tasked Nigerians, including his subjects, to embrace unity, rethink outdated approaches and deliberately build a future anchored on purpose, excellence and collective responsibility.

The monarch gave the task weekend, at a ceremony marking the fifth anniversary of his coronation at Aghofen (palace) in Warri, attended by prominent Nigerians, including top government officials, ministers, fellow traditional rulers, diplomats, captains of industry and military commanders from across the country.

The Olu specifically acknowledged traditional rulers from the North led by the Emir of Zazzau, who represented the Sultan, as well as the Emir of Kano; monarchs from the South-west, including the Alaafin of Oyo, the Olowo of Owo and a representative of the Ooni of Ife; the Eze Arochukwu, who led the traditional rulers from the East; and traditional rulers from Delta State.

“We are deeply inspired by the kindness that God has shown us which calls for all of us to reunite, rally around the crown and the greater purpose we have been entrusted with,” he said.

Atuwatse III stressed the need for the traditional institution to look beyond ceremonial functions and become an instrument for unity, development and inter-generational responsibility, noting that the crown was “not merely an ornament,” but “a carried responsibility to be stewarded, a legacy to be protected and a purpose to be fulfilled together”.

According to him, the strength of a people should not be measured by those excluded, but by the number of people who can be inspired, empowered and united around a common purpose.

“Our strength is not found in the numbers we exclude, but rather in the multitude that can be inspired, empowered and brought together for a common purpose,” the monarch said.

He therefore urged the Itsekiris to put past differences behind and build bridges rather than walls, adding: “We cannot allow past distances to prevent future unity; we must rightly build bridges where necessary and not walls. If our future must be different, the way we do things must change.”

A major thrust of the Olu’s anniversary message was a call for a mindset change in the approach to culture, tradition, leadership and development, noting that while traditions remained important, societies must be willing to examine inherited practices and adapt them to meet the demands of the future.

He drew a distinction between tradition and culture, explaining that culture represents the way people do things, while traditions are practices inherited from the past.

According to him, the past cannot be changed, but the future can be deliberately shaped by the choices people make in the present.
